imprecision.note: Serious events against vapes without nicotine: fewer than 100 events (two levels in the review); against nicotine replacement fewer than 300 events, and any adverse event against NRT: imprecision and I² 72%.

rate.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high; the rating is for the comparisons with nicotine replacement and with vapes without nicotine, and the comparison with support only or no support, which the review rates very low, is labelled in the statement rather than allowed to set the claim's rating (METHODS §6.3; the same approach as the all-cause estimate in the methamphetamine mortality claim). Imprecision, two levels: serious adverse events against vapes without nicotine rest on fewer than 100 events (the review's two levels); against nicotine replacement the review took one level for fewer than 300 events, and for any adverse event against nicotine replacement one level for imprecision and one for inconsistency (I² 72%); all reach low. Risk of bias, not rated down for these two comparisons (the review does not downgrade them; for support only or no support it takes levels for unblinded assessment and differential contact). Indirectness, not rated down: regulated vapes supplied in trials, adults, up to about 2 years. Relation insufficient-evidence because the intervals do not exclude a difference of about 2 serious events in 100 against nicotine replacement and the trials were too short and too small to show rare or later harms (METHODS §6.3: no detectable effect needs an interval that excludes meaningful effects). Status replicated for the main finding, serious events, whose pools have I² 0% in all three comparisons; adverse events overall are less consistent (I² 72% and 58%), which the statement shows. Living review: later updates will change the numbers.
rate.population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes; adverse events 8, 6 and 11 trials (3,107, 909 and 2,801 people) and serious adverse events 10, 11 and 18 trials (4,045, 1,786 and 5,032 people) against nicotine replacement, vapes without nicotine, and support only or no support; follow-up 1 week to about 2 years; Cochrane living review, search to 1 January 2026
rate.comparator: Nicotine replacement therapy; a vape without nicotine; behavioural support only or no support
rate.outcome: Any adverse event and serious adverse event during follow-up of one week or longer (self-report and medical records)
rate.magnitude: Serious adverse events (risk difference; per 100 with comparator vs vape): vs NRT 0.01 (−0.01 to 0.02), 6 vs 7 (5–8), 10 trials, 4,045 participants, moderate; vs non-nicotine vape 0.00 (−0.01 to 0.01), 2 vs 2 (1–3), 11 trials, 1,786, low; vs behavioural support only or no support 0.00 (−0.00 to 0.01), 3 vs 3 (3–4), 18 trials, 5,032, very low. Any adverse event (RR): vs NRT 0.95 (0.72–1.24), 41 vs 39 per 100 (30–51), 8 trials, 3,107, I² 72%, low; vs non-nicotine vape 1.01 (0.95–1.08), 46 vs 46 per 100 (44–50), 6 trials, 909, moderate; vs support only or no support 1.22 (1.00–1.49), 43 vs 52 per 100 (43–64), 11 trials, 2,801, I² 58%, very low. Industry-funded trials left out (Table 2): none to remove against NRT; against a vape without nicotine any adverse event 1.01 (0.95–1.08) and serious events −0.00 (−0.01 to 0.01), unchanged; against support only or no support the review reports no change in reading for serious events, and any adverse event reads 1.26 (0.96–1.66), I² 60%.
rate.short: Nobody can say for sure. In quit-smoking trials, serious health problems were about as common with a nicotine vape as with patches or gum: 7 against 6 in 100.
rate.rate: Chance decided who got a vape, but serious problems were too few to rule out a small difference, and side-effect results varied between trials. The comparison with counselling or no help is weaker still.

risk_of_bias.note: None of the four trials low risk; three high; unblinded arms, unequal interventions; the comparison with continued smoking rests on one high-risk trial.

indirectness.note: Quitting at 4 to 8 weeks only; three trials enrolled people not planning to quit; all participants smoked.

imprecision.note: Five quits in all across the comparisons; intervals from 0.03 to 96.

publication_bias.note: Ten ongoing trials; industry reports not searched; recorded, not rated.

rate.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane systematic review that found no meta-analysis worth pooling (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). Risk of bias, two levels: none of the four trials was at low risk and three were high, with unblinded arms and unequal interventions in the two trials that matter for quitting; the comparison with continued smoking rests on one trial at high risk of bias (the review's two levels). Indirectness, one level: quitting was measured at 4 to 8 weeks, not the 6 months that the claim's question needs, three of the four trials enrolled people not planning to quit, and no trial included people who vape or use other products. Imprecision, two levels: five people had quit across all comparisons, and the risk ratios' intervals run from 0.03 to 96. Inconsistency does not arise (single trials). Publication bias, not rated down but recorded: ten further trials are ongoing and industry reports were not searched. The total of five levels is more than the three available, so the rating is very low; it is not changed by the biomarker result, which is a separate outcome from one tobacco-industry trial (very low), with no independent trial to set beside it. Relation insufficient-evidence (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: the comparison with continued smoking and the comparison with e-cigarettes come from the same trial of 45 people, the higher-against-lower-strength comparison from a registry record of one trial, and the review's plain language summary speaks of two studies behind those comparisons when both come from one trial.
rate.population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined four small randomised trials of oral nicotine pouches (284 people; 7 days to 8 weeks; three trials enrolled people not planning to quit); Cochrane review, search to 13 January 2025; ten further trials ongoing
rate.exposure: Oral nicotine pouches given by the trial
rate.comparator: Continuing to smoke as usual; a nicotine e-cigarette; a lower-strength pouch (and, for side effects only, snus and nicotine gum)
rate.outcome: Not smoking at week 8 (week 4 in one trial); cigarettes per day in people still smoking; serious and other adverse events; NNAL and carboxyhaemoglobin after about a week
rate.magnitude: Quitting (RR; events; participants): pouch vs continued smoking at week 8, 1/18 vs 0/9, RR 1.58 (95% CI 0.07–35.32), 1 trial, 27, very low certainty; pouch vs nicotine e-cigarette at week 8, 1/18 vs 4/18, RR 0.25 (0.03–2.02), 1 trial, 36, low certainty (review's table: 222 per 1,000 with e-cigarettes vs 56 per 1,000 with pouches; about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate, editors' subtraction); higher vs lower strength at week 4, 2/15 vs 0/15, RR 5.00 (0.26–96.13), 1 trial, 30, not graded. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: vs continued smoking MD −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58), 19; vs e-cigarette MD 5.32 (−2.16 to 12.80), 26; higher vs lower strength, log scale MD −0.20 (−0.27 to −0.13), 30. Serious adverse events: none in any arm (3 trials; vs continued smoking 2 trials, 124 participants, very low; vs e-cigarette 1 trial, 26, low; higher vs lower strength 2 trials, 77). Biomarkers vs continued smoking (Rensch 2023, industry-funded, 53 participants): NNAL MD −265.30 ng/g creatinine (−350.64 to −179.96), COHb MD −6.7% (−8.33 to −5.07); very low.
rate.short: Nobody knows yet. Four small trials, with 284 people over 8 weeks at most, couldn't tell whether pouches help people quit or cut down.
rate.rate: Four tiny trials of 8 weeks at most, mostly in people not trying to quit, and people knew what they were given. So few people quit that any gap could be chance.

risk_of_bias.note: The survey is rated some concerns on ROBINS-E (card sc_goniewicz_2018: one time point, a small group that only vaped and was almost entirely people who had smoked, self-reported product use, no device or nicotine content); the 2023 review is rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_hartmann_boyce_2023) and eight of its nine studies are at high risk of bias; the National Academies report and the UK review are provisional on their cards (critically low and low-confidence placeholders, the UK Methods being unread); the UK authors write that most studies had methodological concerns and that many pooled findings came from short industry-funded trials in confinement. Counted once.

inconsistency.note: For the headline contrast (vaping only against smoking only; nitrosamines, carbon monoxide, volatile compounds) every source goes the same way. The size differs (NNAL about 98% lower in the survey, 58% in the pooled analyses; acrolein marker 60% against 71%), which fits the markers, follow-up and the pooling of mixed group definitions (editors' reading). The nicotine contrast and the comparison of people who vape and smoke do diverge (survey and pooled cross-sectional data against confinement studies); they are outside the rating and are stated as mixed.

indirectness.note: Direct for the claim as worded: adults who smoked or had smoked, markers of what reaches the body, studies of one session to about 12 months, devices of 2013 to about 2021. The wording does not extend to disease, to people who have never smoked, to products on sale now or to exposure over years. Parts of the numbers are seen only through reviews (UK pooled analyses, National Academies); the survey was read in full.

imprecision.note: The headline contrasts are large against their intervals (NNAL t = 27.96; pooled carbon monoxide −9.57 ppm, −17.30 to −1.83). The size is imprecise (three studies in the pooled carbon monoxide estimate; 247 people who only vaped in the survey) and is reported with its intervals.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by any source read. The industry-funded trials and the publicly funded survey agree in direction, which limits the concern for the headline contrast.

large_effect.note: Ratios of about 0.02 to 0.4 for the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL, the acrylonitrile and acrolein markers and carbon monoxide, adjusted for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education and other exposures; the remaining biases (earlier smoking in the vaping group, current smoking misreported as vaping only) work toward smaller differences, not larger.

dose_response.note: Within the survey, levels were higher in people who vaped every day than some days and, among people who did both, rose with how often they smoked (exploratory analyses; the supplement was not read); not counted, because the claim concerns the contrast between groups.

plausible_confounding.note: Not applied; the direction of residual confounding differs by contrast.

rate.reasoning: Observational evidence (a cross-sectional survey; non-randomised and some randomized short studies behind the reviews) starts low. Downgraded once for risk of bias; not downgraded again for the same problem in another domain. Upgraded once for a large effect, applied to evidence already rated down for risk of bias: a strict reading, without the upgrade, gives very low, and the gap between the two is the chance that the lower levels are partly produced by who chooses to vape and how they are classified, which the direction of the main biases (toward smaller differences) and the consistency across a survey, short switching studies and four syntheses argue against but do not exclude. The rating applies to the headline contrast only (people who only vaped against people who only smoked, for nitrosamines, carbon monoxide and volatile compounds). The nicotine comparison, the comparison of people who vape and smoke, the metals, the product-content comparison with pharmaceutical nicotine products and the markers of potential harm after switching are less certain and, taken alone, would be rated very low. The reviews' graded judgments (conclusive, substantial, moderate) are their authors' judgments from a different starting point and are reported, not adopted. Funding is set out in the statement: the industry-funded trials are read beside the publicly funded survey and neither is dropped. Overlap: the 2023 review, the UK pooled analyses and the National Academies chapters share primary studies and are not independent replications; the survey is independent of them. Rated as worded: an association in levels of chemicals, which is not a claim about disease.
rate.population: Adults who smoked cigarettes or had smoked them: US adults in the first wave (2013–2014) of the national PATH survey (247 who only vaped, 93% of them had smoked before; 2,411 who only smoked; 792 who did both; 1,655 who had never used tobacco), adults in nine short switching and confinement studies (1,299 people; Greece, Italy, Poland, the UK and the US; one week to 8 months), and the studies pooled by the UK review (2022; 24 to 60 studies per chemical, follow-up from one session to 12 months) and described by the National Academies (2018); people who vape and have never smoked are almost absent
rate.exposure: Vaping (e-cigarettes) as the only product: in the survey, self-reported current use every day or some days and no other tobacco (59% of the group reported nicotine-containing e-cigarettes, as printed); in the switching and confinement studies, being given or switching to an e-cigarette
rate.comparator: Smoking cigarettes only (main comparison); doing both (vaping and smoking); using no tobacco or nicotine (the survey's never-used group; abstainers in one small study)
rate.outcome: Levels of nicotine, tobacco-specific nitrosamines (NNAL), carbon monoxide and other smoke chemicals (volatile compounds, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, metals) measured in urine, breath and blood; short-term markers of potential harm (inflammation, oxidative stress, flow-mediated dilation, heart rate, blood pressure) after switching. These are measures of what reaches the body, not of disease.
rate.magnitude: Against people who only smoke (levels in urine unless stated; absolute values before relative). National survey (PATH, 2013–2014; 247 people who only vaped against 2,411 who only smoked; geometric means per mg creatinine): total nicotine equivalents 2.000 (95% CI 1.100–3.500) against 27.90 (23.80–32.70) nmol, about 93% lower; NNAL 4.887 (3.817–6.257) against 203.5 (181.7–227.9) pg, about 98% lower; acrylonitrile marker 3.959 (3.002–5.219) against 123.9 (109.9–139.7) ng, 97% lower; acrolein marker 108.0 (95.93–121.6) against 271.5 (255.1–289.0) ng, 60% lower; acrylamide marker 56.05 against 136.4 ng, 59% lower; naphthalene marker 62% and pyrene marker 47% lower; cadmium 0.193 against 0.277 ng, 30% lower; nearly all other metals and the toluene, benzene and carbon disulfide markers similar (percentages recomputed by the editors from the printed means, within one point of the text). 2023 systematic review (nine studies, 1,299 adults, one week to 8 months): exhaled carbon monoxide, vaping only against smoking only −9.57 ppm (−17.30 to −1.83; 3 studies); 12 of 13 other biomarkers lower with vaping only, none higher, one (NNN) not different. UK review (McNeill et al., 2022), pooled analyses of people who vaped against people who smoked: NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94% and NNN 90% lower (5 analyses); 3-HPMA 71%, CNEMA 94% and MHBMA 83% lower (15 analyses; formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive); blood carboxyhaemoglobin significantly lower (2 analyses); nicotine and its metabolites not significantly different (5 analyses, against people who smoked at least weekly). Against people who use no tobacco or nicotine: survey, never-used group (1,655 people) against people who only vaped: NNAL 0.921 (0.819–1.035) against 4.887 pg (81% lower), lead 0.351 against 0.432 ng, cadmium 0.149 against 0.193 ng, pyrene marker 0.128 against 0.161 ng, acrylonitrile marker 1.315 against 3.959 ng (about 66% lower); all major nicotine metabolites, all nitrosamines, 4 metals, 1 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon and 4 volatile-compound markers were higher in the group that only vaped. UK review: nitrosamines significantly higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses; nicotine significantly higher in 4; volatile compounds not different in 10 analyses except CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); metals mixed, mostly higher; other toxicants (9 studies, not pooled) higher. One study with an abstinent group: exhaled carbon monoxide at 12 weeks 1 ppm (SD 1) in 16 people who vaped and in 12 who abstained. Against people who both vaped and smoked: survey, both group (792 people) against smoking only: total nicotine equivalents 43.70 (39.80–48.10) against 27.90 nmol; NNAL 262.6 (240.0–287.3) against 203.5 pg; the smoking-only group was lower by 15% for the pyrene marker, 10% for the acrolein marker and 15% for the acrylonitrile marker; lead and cadmium did not differ; cigarettes a day 15.1 against 15.4. Switching studies: exhaled carbon monoxide, vaping only against both −4.40 ppm (−12.04 to 3.24; 2 studies); both against smoking only −1.91 ppm (−3.38 to −0.45; 2 studies); of 25 biomarkers, 12 lower with vaping only, 5 lower with both (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites, one study of 22 people) and 8 not different or inconsistent. Markers of potential harm (UK review): flow-mediated dilation lowered in the short term by both acute vaping and acute smoking and improved by 4 weeks of switching in one randomized trial; C-reactive protein lower than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine in pooled cross-sectional data (3 studies), not confirmed in controlled or longitudinal studies; LDL cholesterol no difference; blood pressure lower than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine in pooled cross-sectional analyses of people who had vaped for at least 3 months or a year; heart rate lower than in people who smoke when the groups were mutually exclusive; pulse wave velocity may fall after a sustained switch (longest follow-up 4 months). Follow-up: a single session to 7 days (acute) or 8 days to 12 months in the UK review; one week to 8 months in the 2023 review; the survey is a single time point.
rate.short: Yes, much less of most. But not clearly less nicotine. In a US survey, people who only vaped had about 98% less of one cancer-linked chemical than people who only smoked.
rate.rate: A survey at one point in time and short switching studies, some paid for by tobacco companies, all point the same way. But most people who vaped had smoked before, and these are chemical levels, not illness.

risk_of_bias.note: Both cohort analyses are rated high on ROBINS-E (cards sc_berlowitz_2022 and sc_xie_2020): residual confounding by smoking history, since most people who vaped had smoked, the heart analysis's reference group includes people who had stopped smoking and the group that only vaped had more pack-years (mean 11.0 against 4.2, spreads several times the means); self-reported, non-adjudicated diagnoses; exposure recorded at the first wave only in the lung analysis. The three reviews are provisional or critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_nasem_2018, sc_banks_2023, sc_mcneill_2022). Counted once.

inconsistency.note: The two analyses answer different questions (heart and lung) and do not conflict; the three reviews agree that clinical outcomes have not been studied, and the cohort results do not contradict them.

indirectness.note: Direct for the claim as worded (newly reported diagnoses in adults over up to four years, and what reviews found). The wording does not reach cancer, people who have never smoked, longer use or current devices, and says so.

imprecision.note: Only 41 (any heart disease or stroke) and 15 (heart attack, heart failure or stroke) events occurred among people who only vaped, so the hazard ratios 1.00 (0.69–1.45) and 1.35 (0.75–2.42) fit a lower rate, no change or a clearly higher rate; the intervals for single lung conditions are wide (for example asthma, current use 1.32, 1.01–1.72).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable. Both cohort analyses use data from one federally funded study and declare no tobacco or vape industry funding; the reviews are reported as they state their own evidence.

large_effect.note: The lung ratios (about 1.2 to 1.7) are modest and fell sharply when smoking history was added; the heart ratio for people who only vaped is 1.00. No upgrade.

dose_response.note: Exploratory highest rates with every-day use, first use before age 25 and established use (values in a supplement not read); not counted.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding by smoking more plausibly raises the lung ratios, while reverse causation (people with early symptoms switching to vaping) could hide an association; no upgrade.

rate.reasoning: Observational cohorts start low. Downgraded once for risk of bias (both analyses rated high on ROBINS-E) and once for imprecision (few events in people who only vaped), which reaches the floor, very low. Rated as worded: the claim is that the evidence is insufficient to say whether vaping changes the risk of heart or lung disease, not that vaping has no effect; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The three reviews' judgments (no available evidence, insufficient evidence, low or very low certainty) are their authors' judgments and are reported, not adopted. Overlap: the heart and lung analyses are two analyses of one cohort that share data and some authors, so they are not independent replications; the reviews overlap in the studies they draw on. The acute lung injury outbreak (EVALI) is outside the rating: the Australian review judged it conclusive, largely with THC-containing products. A published critique of the Australian review (Mendelsohn et al., 2022) disputes its comparison group and standards of evidence but brings no data on disease rates, so it changes no rating. Funding is set out in the statement: no tobacco or vape industry funding is declared for the cohort analyses or the reviews read; the pharmaceutical and device-company ties of some authors are listed as printed, and the sponsors of the studies in the National Academies report are in an online table that was not read.
rate.population: US adults in the national PATH cohort followed from 2013–2014 for up to about four years: 24,027 with no heart disease or stroke at the start (heart analysis, Waves 1 to 5) and 21,618 with no asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis at the start (lung analysis, Waves 1 to 4); most of the people who vaped had smoked (in the lung analysis 16.0% of those currently vaping had never smoked cigarettes); and the reviews of the wider literature by the National Academies (2018), the UK government (2022; search to July 2021) and the Australian government (2023; studies to July 2020, major reviews to December 2021)
rate.exposure: Vaping (e-cigarette use): current use of any frequency, updated at each wave (heart analysis), or ever, former or current use at the first wave only (lung analysis), with or without smoking
rate.comparator: People who used neither cigarettes nor e-cigarettes (the heart analysis's reference group, which includes people who had stopped smoking); people who only smoked cigarettes; people who both vaped and smoked; in the lung analysis, people who had never used an e-cigarette (including people who smoked)
rate.outcome: Newly reported, self-reported diagnoses of heart disease or stroke (heart analysis) and of asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis (lung analysis) over up to about four years; and what three reviews concluded about heart disease, lung disease and cancer
rate.magnitude: Absolute counts and rates before ratios. Heart (Berlowitz et al., 2022; PATH Waves 1 to 5; 24,027 adults with no heart disease at the start; up to 4 years): new self-reported diagnosis of heart disease or stroke in 764 of 14,832 people who used neither product, 41 of 822 who only vaped, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both (counts only; the groups differ in age and follow-up); age-adjusted rates as printed per 1,000 person-years 8.0, 9.7, 14.8 and 17.1 in that order (not reproducible from the counts). Hazard ratios against using neither, fully adjusted: only vaping 1.00 (0.69–1.45), only smoking 1.53 (1.30–1.79), both 1.54 (1.21–1.96); for heart attack, heart failure or stroke (519 cases, 15 among people who only vaped) 1.35 (0.75–2.42), 2.20 (1.73–2.81) and 2.08 (1.40–3.09). Against people who only smoked: only vaping 0.66 (0.46–0.94) and 0.61 (0.34–1.09); both 1.01 (0.81–1.26) and 0.94 (0.65–1.36). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone, only vaping against neither 1.16 (0.82–1.66) and 1.55 (0.87–2.76). Lungs (Xie et al., 2020; PATH Waves 1 to 4; 21,618 adults with no respiratory condition at the start; up to about 4 years): 1,460 (6.8%) with at least one new diagnosis (asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948 new diagnoses); adjusted rate per 1,000 person-years for any condition: never used 20.41 (18.65–22.17), ever 26.06 (22.63–29.49), former 26.12, current 26.68 (21.83–31.52) (about 2.0 against 2.6–2.7 in 100 a year, editors' conversion); for single conditions, never against ever: COPD 6.48 against 10.49, emphysema 3.74 against 5.76, chronic bronchitis 12.18 against 16.23, asthma 10.73 against 13.31. Rate ratios against never use (fully adjusted, ever / former / current): any condition 1.28 (1.10–1.48) / 1.28 (1.09–1.51) / 1.31 (1.08–1.59); chronic bronchitis 1.33 / 1.31 / 1.33; emphysema 1.54 / 1.42 / 1.69; COPD 1.62 / 1.66 / 1.57; asthma 1.24 (1.01–1.53) / 1.19 (0.95–1.50) / 1.32 (1.01–1.72). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone the ratios for ever use were 2.14 (any condition), 4.02 (emphysema) and 5.03 (COPD). Among people with good or better self-rated health (18,649): former 1.21 (1.00–1.47), current 1.43 (1.14–1.80); among people with no chronic condition at baseline (14,865): ever 1.20 (0.99–1.45), former 1.11 (0.90–1.37), current 1.40 (1.09–1.79). Reviews (the authors' own gradings): National Academies 2018 conclusions 9-1 (clinical cardiovascular outcomes, no available evidence), 11-1 (respiratory disease, no available evidence), 10-1 (intermediate cancer endpoints, no available evidence), 18-3 (long-term illness or death in people who vape and smoke, no available evidence), 11-4 (cough and wheeze in adolescents, moderate), 11-2 and 11-3 (adults with asthma or COPD who switch, limited); UK review 2022: clinical cardiovascular outcomes still no available evidence, cardiovascular risk uncertain, lung tests insufficient, no cancer incidence data; Australian review 2023: clinical cardiovascular outcomes and invasive cancer no available evidence, asthma, bronchitis and COPD insufficient in people who smoke and no available evidence in people who do not, certainty low or very low, EVALI conclusive (14% of cases in the largest study reported only nicotine products, 2% only non-nicotine products). Follow-up: up to 4 years in both cohort analyses; the reviews' evidence mostly concerns short-term effects.
rate.short: Nobody can say yet. A big US study found no clear rise in heart disease in people who only vaped, and more lung problems that past smoking may explain.
rate.rate: Two analyses of one US study, based on illnesses people reported, with few heart cases among people who only vaped. Most who vaped had smoked, and nobody was followed past 4 years.

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional self-report comparisons (card sc_liu_2017: ROBINS-E overall high). The e-cigarette group is selected (nearly all had formerly smoked; few of those who try e-cigarettes use them daily) and prior tobacco history, length of use and amount per day are not adjusted for; one item is a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes. The other surveys are read only through the National Academies' account, which itself flags a non-representative web sample with recall of earlier smoking.

inconsistency.note: Every source read points the same way; the size of the gap differs by item and survey.

indirectness.note: The data are from surveys of 2012–2014, before newer products such as nicotine-salt liquids and disposables were common (the National Academies call generalizability to products of that time questionable, and the UK and Australian reviews list newer products and dependence by product type as little studied); several sources are second-hand, and the UK review's dependence statements restate National Academies and earlier reports (counted once, as are the two PATH analyses).

imprecision.note: Intervals on the adjusted odds ratios exclude 1; the smallest e-cigarette groups are 124 and 156 people.

large_effect.note: Adjusted odds ratios are 2.85 to 6.92, but the biases that remain (selection of people who stay with e-cigarettes after smoking; prior tobacco history not adjusted) run away from the null, so no upgrade.

rate.reasoning: Observational (cross-sectional survey) evidence starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. The National Academies rate the lower-dependence comparison moderate and the dependence finding substantial, and the UK review repeats those ratings; these are the authors' judgments over mixed study types, not a GRADE rating, and overlapping reports and the two PATH analyses are counted once. Status replicated rests on independent datasets (US telephone survey, PATH, a web survey, English youth surveys) that agree on direction, three of them known here only through the reviews.
rate.population: Adults in the United States who used only e-cigarettes, or only cigarettes, every day (PATH Wave 1, 2013–2014); young people aged 11 to 19 in England (2021 surveys); other adult surveys as described by the National Academies
rate.outcome: Dependence symptoms (self-rated dependence, strong cravings, difficulty keeping from using where prohibited, feeling a need to use, time to first use after waking) and dependence index scores
rate.magnitude: Daily e-cigarette-only (n = 156) vs daily cigarette-only (n = 3,430), PATH Wave 1, weighted: self-rated dependence 77.2% vs 94.0% (adjusted odds ratio for the cigarette group 6.92, 95% CL 4.46–10.73); strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9% (2.85, 1.92–4.23); difficulty keeping from using where prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6% (6.39, 2.85–14.32); felt they really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5% (3.89, 2.36–6.40); time to first use after waking, adjusted geometric mean 29.16 (24.39–34.87) vs 20.03 (18.66–21.49) minutes (editors' calculation: ratio 1.46). As described by the National Academies: US National Adult Tobacco Survey 2012–2013, daily e-cigarette-only n = 124 vs cigarette-only n = 3,963, every symptom less common in the e-cigarette group (for example use within 30 minutes of waking 46.1%, 35.1–57.4); PATH Wave 1 item-response index, e-cigarette-only (n = 437) 1.37 SD units below cigarette-only (n = 8,689); web survey of 3,609 people who vaped daily, index 8.1 vs 14.5 for recalled smoking. England 2021, 16–19-year-olds: rated themselves a little or very dependent 52.5% of those who vaped vs 83% of those who smoked (McNeill et al., 2022).
rate.short: Less, it seems, but still common. In a US survey, 77 in 100 adults who only vaped daily said they felt dependent, against 94 in 100 who only smoked daily.
rate.rate: One-time surveys of what people said, with no follow-up. Nearly all who vaped had smoked before, past smoking wasn't allowed for, and the data predate newer vapes like disposables.

risk_of_bias.note: Small, mostly single-session studies (4 to 37 volunteers in chambers; 5 people living with someone who vaped), read here through the National Academies' and the UK review's descriptions, which cannot be appraised from the summaries; the one primary source read in full (card sc_visser_2019, 17 volunteers and a model with worst-case assumptions) is rated high risk of bias on the editors' checklist.

inconsistency.note: The exposure findings point the same way; levels differ with setting and number of people vaping (one home study found a median similar to a control home despite real-time rises), which the sources explain by exposure conditions.

indirectness.note: The outcome of interest, health of people nearby, was not measured; air and cotinine measures and a model stand in for it. Chambers and conventions differ from everyday rooms, and the studies are mostly from 2014–2017, with the devices of that period.

imprecision.note: Small samples are counted under risk of bias.

rate.reasoning: Observational and laboratory exposure evidence starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on health effects, which is what the sources support: the National Academies, the UK review and the Australian review all say that health effects of second-hand vapour have not been measured or cannot be concluded. The National Academies' conclusive rating concerns the rise in airborne particles and nicotine, not harm. Status replicated applies to that exposure finding, shown by independent studies in different settings.
rate.population: People who do not vape who are near someone vaping (volunteers in chambers and rooms, people living with someone who vapes, people at vaping conventions); 17 adults who vaped daily whose breath was measured (Netherlands)
rate.exposure: Breathing air in which someone has vaped (second-hand vapour)
rate.comparator: The same air without vaping (background), and, in four studies, air with cigarette smoke
rate.outcome: Health effects in people nearby (not measured in any study read); exposure measures: airborne nicotine, fine particles and other chemicals, and nicotine biomarkers
rate.magnitude: Health effects in people nearby: not measured in any study read. Exposure, as the National Academies describe the studies (vaping against baseline or control): chamber with 5 people vaping, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 (SD 2.49) vs undetectable µg/m3 and PM2.5 152 (86.8) vs 32.4 µg/m3; 9 volunteers for 2 hours in a café-like room, PM2.5 197 vs 6 µg/m3 and nicotine 2.2 vs below 0.04 µg/m3; 37 volunteers over 4 hours, nicotine 0.38 to 2.83 µg/m3 (several-fold below workplace limits); homes of people living with someone vaping more than 2 hours a day vs control homes, median air nicotine 0.11 vs 0.01 µg/m3, salivary cotinine 0.24 vs 0.05 ng/mL, urinary cotinine 2.64 vs 0.72 ng/mL; convention, estimated 24-hour PM10 1,800 µg/m3. Against second-hand cigarette smoke: one chamber, airborne nicotine 3.32 vs 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 151.7 vs 819.3 µg/m3 (stated as 10 and 7 times; editors' calculation from the raw means 9.5 and 5.4 times); homes, airborne nicotine 0.13 vs 0.74 µg/m3 (5.7 times) and salivary cotinine 0.19 vs 0.38 ng/mL; surface nicotine 7.7 vs 1,303 µg/m2 (found in half of 8 vaping homes vs all 6 smoking homes). UK review: 6 biomarker studies, none from the UK; short exposures no detectable change. Dutch measurement and model (Visser et al., 2019): first breath after one puff, nicotine median 108 ng (below the limit to 2,140 ng), propylene glycol seen in 4 of 17, glycerol in none, nitrosamines up to 77 pg (NDMA equivalent); modelled car / office: nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3, propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; margins 2.1 / 6 (nicotine, heart rate and blood pressure), 17 / 74–81 (propylene glycol, irritation), 521 / 2,297 (nitrosamines, against 10,000).
rate.short: Nobody knows yet. None of the studies we read checked the health of people nearby. Vaping does add nicotine and tiny particles to the air, but less than cigarette smoke.
rate.rate: Small, short studies of the air and of a few people's body levels, mostly from 2014 to 2017, plus computer models. None of the studies we read measured the health of people nearby.

risk_of_bias.note: The 95% figure began as an expert rating (known here only through the editorial's account); the UK review's pooled biomarker results include many tobacco-industry-funded confinement trials of up to 7 days and most of its studies had methodological concerns; the National Academies' human studies were mostly small and several tested a manufacturer's own product (the chapter does not say who funded them); the editorial, the 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary appraise nothing (cards sc_eissenberg_2020, sc_mckee_2015 and sc_mendelsohn_2022: overall high) and the Australian review applies a precautionary principle and excluded biomarker studies. The reviews are read as summaries, not at the study level.

inconsistency.note: Counted once, under risk of bias: the sides read a largely shared body of evidence differently and answer different questions (exposure and short-term measures against clinical outcomes and starting to smoke); the exposure findings themselves point the same way.

indirectness.note: The question is lifetime harm (disease and death). What is measured is exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements (single sessions to 12 months in the UK review; to about two years in the National Academies' studies) and expert ratings; products have changed since most of the studies and newer ones are little studied.

imprecision.note: No estimate of harm is pooled, so precision is not rated.

rate.reasoning: Observational, indirect evidence (exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements and expert judgement) starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on the size of the difference, which is what the sources support, with the direction (lower exposure to smoke toxicants) reported beside it. The National Academies' conclusive and substantial ratings concern exposure and short-term outcomes in people who switched completely, not lifetime harm; the UK review's statement is an expert judgment on a body of evidence that reaches only 12 months, as its authors say, and the Australian review's reading rests on a different set of evidence. Overlapping reports are counted once. The 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary, read in full (McKee & Capewell, 2015; Mendelsohn et al., 2022), add arguments about where the figure came from and which comparison matters, not measurements, and change no rating.
rate.population: Adults who smoke or have smoked and who vape or switch completely to vaping (mostly short studies); people who have never smoked and who vape; as covered by two government-commissioned reviews, a National Academies report, an editorial, a 2015 analysis article and a 2022 commentary
rate.exposure: Vaping nicotine e-cigarettes (alone, or replacing smoking completely)
rate.comparator: Continuing to smoke cigarettes; and, as a second comparison, using no nicotine product
rate.outcome: Overall harm to health, disease and death (not measured in any source read); what was measured instead: levels of chemicals in the body, short-term lung, heart and blood-pressure measures, laboratory emissions, and expert ratings
rate.magnitude: Not estimable from the sources read: none gives the rate of any disease or death in people who only vape, against people who smoke or people who use no nicotine. The figure in dispute: vaping at least 95% less harmful than smoking, that is smoking at least 20 times more harmful, stated in the UK 2015 report and described in 2022 as broadly accurate over the short and medium term (McNeill et al., 2022); described as arising from a July 2013 rating by 12 experts of 12 products on 14 criteria (Eissenberg et al., 2020; the rating itself not read), and as coming from a single meeting of 12 people who built a multicriteria decision analysis model of their opinions (McKee & Capewell, 2015). Estimate cited on the other side: lifetime cancer risk from vaping less than 0.5% of that from smoking, modelled from what aerosol contains (two studies cited by Mendelsohn et al., 2022; not read). Measured, people who vape against people who smoke (UK review, pooled analyses): nitrosamine breakdown products NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower; acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower; blood carboxyhaemoglobin lower; nicotine not different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; metals mixed. Against people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher; volatile organic compounds not significantly different except CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses (past smoking not separable); metals mostly higher. As described by the National Academies: smoke constituents 9- to 450-fold higher than aerosol (15 puffs assumed equal to one cigarette; Goniewicz et al., 2014); toxicants 82% to more than 99% lower per puff (Margham et al., 2016); about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents in smoke (Tayyarah and Long, 2014); 4 of 11 metals higher in one aerosol than in smoke (Williams et al., 2013); in people who switched, urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower after 5 days (105 people), NNAL down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks (20 people); all but one of the human studies showed short-term improvement, none showed more harm among people who switched. Follow-up: the UK review could summarise at most 12 months; the Australian review found no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease (21 studies) or invasive cancer (1 study).
rate.short: Nobody has measured it yet. People who vape take in much less of many smoke chemicals than people who smoke. But the famous claim that it's 95% less harmful is disputed.
rate.rate: The sources we read give no long-term counts of illness or death. The figures rest on chemical levels, short studies (many of the chemical ones paid for by tobacco companies) and expert opinion.

risk_of_bias.note: Participants could not be blinded to exercising and the outcome is a self-rating taken minutes later; the trials' risk of bias was not assessed; most trials are by the review's authors.

inconsistency.note: All trials favour exercise, but the size ranges from about 0.2 to 4.5 points (I² 92% to 94%), only partly explained by the kind of exercise.

indirectness.note: Worded for the population and timing studied (temporary abstinence, craving minutes after exercise); quitting is not claimed.

publication_bias.note: Unpublished theses were included and gave similar results; no small-study test; not downgraded.

rate.reasoning: Randomized trials start high. Risk of bias −1 (unblinded self-rated outcome, no appraisal of the trials, trials mostly by the review's authors) and inconsistency −1 (a tenfold range in size) give low. Worded as an association because the size, and how much of it is exercise rather than expectation, are uncertain, although the design is randomized. Status replicated: 19 trials from several research groups point the same way; agreement with an earlier aggregate meta-analysis (Roberts et al., 2012) is not counted as independent because the trials overlap.
rate.population: Adults who smoke, abstaining for at least 2 hours in laboratory studies, not using nicotine replacement or in a cessation programme, mostly not trying to quit
rate.exposure: A single short bout of physical activity, mostly moderate walking or cycling (study conditions in the study card)
rate.comparator: Sitting quietly or another passive condition (listening, a video, a cognitive task, body scanning)
rate.outcome: Self-rated strength of desire to smoke and desire to smoke (single 7-point items) immediately or 5 minutes after the bout, adjusted for the rating before
rate.magnitude: Two-stage random-effects IPD meta-analysis: strength of desire −1.91 points (95% CI −2.59 to −1.22), 15 trials, 797 observations, I² 94.2%; desire to smoke −2.03 (−2.60 to −1.46), 17 trials, 837 observations, I² 92.0%. One-stage model: −1.89 and −2.03, with 95% of trials' true effects expected between −3.56 and −0.22 and between −3.45 and −0.62. Single trials −0.22 to −4.54.
rate.short: Right afterwards, it seems to. In 19 trials, people rated their urge about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale after a short walk or bike ride than after sitting still.
rate.rate: 19 trials all point the same way, but people knew they had exercised and rated their own urge, the size varied a lot, and most trials involved the review's own authors.

risk_of_bias.note: Five trials kept people who smoked again in the analyses, attrition was high and sometimes unequal, one comparator contained nicotine, and blinding was not assessed.

inconsistency.note: Irritability and total discomfort are consistent; the mixed symptoms are reported as mixed.

indirectness.note: Worded for the products, people and first week studied.

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed; the statement says sizes are unknown.

publication_bias.note: Counts of significant results in published trials, with blanks that may hide unreported null results, in a manufacturer-funded review.

rate.reasoning: Randomized placebo-controlled trials start high. Risk of bias −1 and publication or reporting bias −1 give low. The claim gives directions only; the size of any reduction is unknown. Status replicated: all nine trials that reported irritability, from several groups, agree, as do six of seven for total withdrawal; craving with gum is not replicated (3 of 7).
rate.population: Adults who smoked (mostly moderate to heavy smoking), without psychiatric or acute physical illness, who stopped in placebo-controlled trials published 1984 to 2000
rate.exposure: Oral nicotine products: nicotine gum, inhaler or sublingual tablet (study conditions in the study card)
rate.comparator: A placebo product of the same kind (low-nicotine gum in one trial)
rate.outcome: Withdrawal symptoms and craving in the first week of abstinence, counted as significant or not in each trial
rate.magnitude: No effect sizes. Fractions of trials with a significant reduction: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11 (gum 3/7; inhaler 3/3; tablet 1/1), poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, hunger 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2.
rate.short: For some symptoms, it seems so. In 12 older trials, people on nicotine gum, an inhaler or a tablet were less grumpy in the first week than on a dummy.
rate.rate: Old trials where chance decided who got nicotine. But the review counted only which trials found a difference, unreported results may hide ones that found none, and a drug company paid for it.

item.statement: In quit-smoking trials, vapes clearly did more serious harm than patches or gum.
item.why: No clear difference showed up: 7 against 6 in 100 had serious problems. But problems were few, and the trials lasted about 2 years at most, too short to show rare or later harms.

lines.short: Nobody can say for sure. In quit-smoking trials, serious health problems were about as common with a nicotine vape as with patches or gum: 7 against 6 in 100.
lines.but: Serious problems were few, and the trials lasted about 2 years at most. That's too few and too short to show rare or later harms.
how: A review of trials, searched up to January 2026, looked at adults who smoked and were given regulated nicotine vapes to help them stop. They were followed for 1 week to about 2 years. The review says this doesn't apply to people who never smoked, and that cannabis or illicit vapes may carry different harms.

Serious health problems: 7 in 100 with a vape against 6 in 100 with patches, gum or similar (10 trials, 4,045 people), and 2 in 100 in both groups against a vape without nicotine (11 trials, 1,786 people). Side effects of any kind were about as common too: 39 against 41 in 100, and 46 against 46.

Against counselling only or no help, the evidence is weaker. Serious problems: 3 in 100 in both groups (18 trials, 5,032 people; 10 of them recorded none). Side effects of any kind: 52 in 100 with a vape against 43, though the range includes no difference.

Some trials found more throat or mouth irritation, cough or dry mouth with vapes; others found fewer breathing symptoms. One found more nausea with patches, gum or similar. No trial against those was paid for by the tobacco or vape industry; one or two in each of the others were, and leaving them out didn't change what the review concluded.

item.statement: Trials show that nicotine pouches help people quit smoking.
item.why: Nobody knows yet: four small trials of 8 weeks at most couldn't tell. Three of them took people who weren't planning to quit.

lines.short: Nobody knows yet. Four small trials, with 284 people over 8 weeks at most, couldn't tell whether pouches help people quit or cut down.
lines.but: Three of the four trials took people who weren't planning to quit. None compared pouches with patches or gum for quitting.
how: A review of trials, searched up to January 2025, found only four small ones in adults who smoked: 284 people, followed for 7 days to 8 weeks. Ten more trials are under way.

In one trial of 45 people, 1 of 18 given pouches had quit at week 8. That compares with 0 of 9 who kept smoking as usual and 4 of 18 given a nicotine vape. None of these gaps, or those in cigarettes a day, can be told from chance, and the trial had serious design flaws.
No serious health problems were recorded in the three trials that reported them, over 1 to 8 weeks. Other side effects were reported in different ways and were mostly mild or uncommon.

A trial paid for by a tobacco company tested 53 people after about a week. Those on pouches had less carbon monoxide in blood, and less of a tobacco chemical in urine, than those who kept smoking. No other trial measured these.

item.statement: If you vape, you take in as many harmful chemicals as if you smoked.
item.why: Much less of most: in a US survey, about 98% less of one cancer-linked chemical, though nicotine wasn't clearly lower. These are chemical levels, not illness.

lines.short: Yes, much less of most. But not clearly less nicotine. In a US survey, people who only vaped had about 98% less of one cancer-linked chemical than people who only smoked.
lines.but: These are chemical levels, not illness. And people who both vaped and smoked didn't have the lower levels.
how: A US survey in 2013 and 2014 compared 247 adults who only vaped (93 in 100 had smoked before) with 2,411 who only smoked. Those who only vaped had about 98% less of a cancer-linked tobacco chemical in their urine and 30% to 97% less of some others. Most metals and a few other chemicals didn't differ.

Short studies where people switched to vaping found the same for carbon monoxide and most other chemicals. So did reviews for the UK in 2022 and by a US expert panel in 2018. Some of those studies were paid for by tobacco companies, but the survey, paid for with public money, agrees.

In the survey, nicotine was 93% lower, but only 59 in 100 of those who only vaped said their vapes had nicotine. In the UK review's pooled studies, nicotine didn't clearly differ. The US panel judged that adults used to vaping take in about as much as from cigarettes.

People who only vaped still had more of some chemicals than people who used no tobacco or nicotine. In the survey, people who both vaped and smoked had as much as people who only smoked, or more, at about the same number of cigarettes a day. Most who vaped had smoked for years, and no study looked past about a year.

item.why: In a US survey, people who both vaped and smoked had as much as people who only smoked, or more, at about the same number of cigarettes a day.

item.statement: Studies have shown that vaping causes heart disease.
item.why: Nobody can say yet. In a big US study, people who only vaped had no clear rise in heart disease over 4 years at most, but only 41 of them got it: too few to be sure either way.

lines.short: Nobody can say yet. A big US study found no clear rise in heart disease in people who only vaped, and more lung problems that past smoking may explain.
lines.but: It's one study, of illnesses people reported themselves, over 4 years at most. Only 41 people who only vaped got heart disease, too few to be sure either way.
how: The study followed about 24,000 US adults for up to 4 years. New heart disease or stroke was reported by 41 of 822 who only vaped, 764 of 14,832 who used neither, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both. The groups differed in age and time followed, so these counts aren't rates.

Allowing for age, health and past smoking, people who only vaped didn't clearly differ from people who used neither, while those who smoked, or smoked and vaped, had about 1.5 times the rate. But the group who used neither included people who had quit smoking, and those who only vaped had smoked more in the past.

In the same study, new lung conditions such as asthma or COPD came to about 2.6 in 100 people a year among those who had ever vaped, against 2.0 among those who never had. Most who vaped had smoked, and without allowing for past smoking the gap looked far bigger. The authors say this can't show that vaping caused it.

Three reviews were done for the US, UK and Australian governments. They found no evidence, or too little, on heart attack, stroke, long-term lung disease or cancer from vaping. The Australian one judged that vapes did cause a lung injury outbreak (EVALI), mostly vapes with THC.

item.statement: Most adults who vape every day, and don't smoke, say they feel dependent.
item.why: In a US survey, 77 in 100 adults who only vaped daily said so, against 94 in 100 who only smoked daily. The survey is from 2013 to 2014, and nearly all had smoked before.

lines.short: Less, it seems, but still common. In a US survey, 77 in 100 adults who only vaped daily said they felt dependent, against 94 in 100 who only smoked daily.
lines.but: Nearly all who vaped had smoked before. And the survey is from 2013 to 2014, before disposables and newer liquids were common.
how: A US survey in 2013 and 2014 compared 156 adults who only vaped daily with 3,430 who only smoked daily. Fewer who vaped said they had strong cravings (73 against 87 in 100) or found it hard to go without where it was banned (6 against 29 in 100).

They also waited longer after waking to first use it: about 29 minutes against 20, on average. The question about places where it's banned fits vaping less well. And there's no agreed way to compare the two.

Other US surveys pointed the same way, and so did surveys of young people in England in 2021. There, about half of 16- to 19-year-olds who vaped felt a little or very dependent, against 83 in 100 who smoked. In one web survey, bigger, more advanced vapes and liquids with more nicotine went with higher dependence scores.

A US expert panel judged that vaping can lead to signs of dependence, and, less firmly, that the risk is lower than with smoking. An Australian review was surer of this for people who don't smoke than for those who do. Each survey was a one-time look, and nobody followed people over time.

item.statement: People who vape daily feel just as addicted as people who smoke daily.
item.why: Fewer reported signs of dependence in a US survey: 73 in 100 adults who only vaped daily had strong cravings, against 87 in 100 who only smoked daily. It's what people said, and nearly all who vaped had smoked before.

item.statement: Vaping indoors leaves the air as clean as before.
item.why: Studies found more nicotine and tiny particles in the air, though less than with cigarette smoke. None of the studies we read checked whether that harms people nearby.

lines.short: Nobody knows yet. None of the studies we read checked the health of people nearby. Vaping does add nicotine and tiny particles to the air, but less than cigarette smoke.
lines.but: The studies were small and short, minutes to hours, mostly from 2014 to 2017. Nobody followed people nearby for weeks or years.
how: In test rooms, homes and a vaping convention, studies found more nicotine and tiny particles in the air when people vaped, a US expert panel says. The more people vaped, the higher the levels. An Australian review found too little proof to say if these levels harm health.

In one home study, 5 people who didn't smoke lived with someone who vaped. Their saliva and urine held more of a nicotine breakdown product than those of people in homes without vaping. A UK review of six studies found no change after short exposures, but rises after long, heavy vaping nearby.

Vaping gave lower levels than smoking in all four studies that compared the two: in one test room, about a tenth of the nicotine and a fifth of the tiny particles. The US panel says nobody knows what that means for health. It adds that children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may be at special risk.

A Dutch team measured the breath of 17 people after one puff, then worked out worst cases on a computer. Safety margins were small for some chemicals, like nicotine in a car, but the team called the effects fairly mild. Nothing was measured in a real room, car or person nearby.

item.statement: The famous figure that vaping is 95% less harmful comes from long-term health studies.
item.why: No study we read tracked illness or death for years in people who only vape against people who smoke. Critics say the figure began as the views of 12 people at one meeting in 2013; a UK review says it still broadly fits the short and medium term.

lines.short: Nobody has measured it yet. People who vape take in much less of many smoke chemicals than people who smoke. But the famous claim that it's 95% less harmful is disputed.
lines.but: No study we read tracked illness or death for years in people who only vape against people who smoke. It all rests on chemical levels, short studies and what experts think.
how: In a UK review, people who vape had much lower levels of many smoke chemicals than people who smoke. Signs of one family of tobacco chemicals were 58% to 94% lower. A US expert panel found that people who fully switched from smoking did better on short-term lung, heart and mouth checks in all but one of 15 studies.

The UK review was done for the government. It says its 2015 figure, that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking, still broadly fits the short and medium term. It now prefers to say vaping carries a small share of smoking's risks, but grants it isn't risk-free, most of all for people who never smoked.

Critics in 2015 and 2020 say the figure came from the views of 12 people at one meeting in 2013, whose own paper admitted a lack of hard evidence. The 2020 critics say vapes have changed too much to rely on it. Still, they grant that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco nitrosamines.

An Australian review says comparing with smoking can't show what vaping does by itself. A 2022 critique says that's the comparison that matters. Against using no nicotine at all, the UK review found harmful exposure the same or higher.

item.statement: In studies, a short walk eased the urge to smoke, compared with sitting still.
item.why: In 19 small trials, the urge was about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale right afterwards. It was rated only minutes later, and people knew they'd exercised.

lines.short: Right afterwards, it seems to. In 19 trials, people rated their urge about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale after a short walk or bike ride than after sitting still.
lines.but: The urge was rated only once, minutes later, and people knew they had exercised. No study here checked whether it helps people quit.
how: A review pooled 19 small trials in adults who smoke. They hadn't smoked for at least 2 hours, weren't using patches, gum or similar, and mostly weren't trying to quit. They did a short bout of exercise, mostly walking or cycling at a moderate pace, or sat quietly instead.

Right afterwards, people rated their urge to smoke about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale. Every trial pointed the same way, but the size ranged from a fraction of a point to more than 4. Tensing muscles while sitting showed among the smallest effects.
The urge was rated only once, right after or 5 minutes later. So these trials can't say how long the drop lasts, or whether it helps people stop or stay stopped.

People knew whether they had exercised, and the review didn't check how well the trials were run. 17 of the 19 trials list at least one of the review's authors. The review used its own institutions' money, and its authors report no tobacco or drug-company ties.

item.statement: In trials, people on nicotine gum and the like felt less grumpy in their first week off smoking.
item.why: All 9 trials that checked found less grumpiness in the first week than with a dummy version. The review gave no sizes, and a drug company paid for it.

lines.short: For some symptoms, it seems so. In 12 older trials, people on nicotine gum, an inhaler or a tablet were less grumpy in the first week than on a dummy.
lines.but: The review only counted which trials found a difference, not how big it was. And a drug company paid for it.
how: A 2001 review gathered 12 trials from 1984 to 2000, with 15 to 240 people each. Most had smoked a fair amount or a lot. After stopping, they got nicotine gum (8 trials), an inhaler (3) or a tablet under the tongue (1), or a dummy version (in one trial, low-nicotine gum).

People on nicotine felt less grumpy than on a dummy in all 9 trials that measured it. Overall discomfort was lower in 6 of 7, anxiety in 3 of 4, and low mood in the one trial that checked it. Results were mixed for restlessness, poor focus, sleep problems and hunger.
Cravings were lower in 7 of 11 trials: all 4 trials of the inhaler or tablet, but only 3 of the 7 gum trials.

Trials that didn't report a symptom left blanks, which may hide results that found no difference. Nothing is known past the first week, no lozenge trial was found, and patches and nasal sprays weren't included.

lines.statement: In adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes (Cochrane living review, searched to 1 January 2026; follow-up from 1 week to about 2 years), the evidence is insufficient to say whether a nicotine vape, compared with nicotine replacement or with a vape without nicotine, changes the risk of serious or other adverse events: no clear difference was seen, but events were few. Serious adverse events: 7 against 6 in 100 with a vape against nicotine replacement (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.02; 10 trials, 4,045 people; moderate certainty) and 2 against 2 in 100 against a vape without nicotine (0.00, −0.01 to 0.01; 11 trials, 1,786 people; low certainty, fewer than 100 events). Any adverse event: 39 against 41 in 100 against nicotine replacement (risk ratio 0.95, 0.72 to 1.24; 8 trials, 3,107 people; low certainty; I² 72%) and 46 against 46 in 100 against a vape without nicotine (1.01, 0.95 to 1.08; 6 trials, 909 people; moderate certainty). Against behavioural support only or no support the certainty is very low: serious events 3 against 3 in 100 (0.00, −0.00 to 0.01; 18 trials, 5,032 people; 10 of the 18 trials recorded none) and any adverse event 52 against 43 in 100 (risk ratio 1.22, 1.00 to 1.49, an interval that touches no difference; 11 trials, 2,801 people). No trial in the comparisons with nicotine replacement had tobacco or vaping industry funding; one or two trials in each of the other two comparisons did, and leaving them out did not change the review's reading of any of these results (for any adverse event against support only or no support the risk ratio then read 1.26, 0.96 to 1.66). Trials that could not be pooled reported more throat or mouth irritation, cough or dry mouth with vapes in some trials and fewer breathing symptoms in others, and more nausea with nicotine replacement in one. The trials used regulated nicotine vapes in adults for up to about 2 years; the review says longer-term effects are unknown, that its conclusion relates to people using regulated vapes to stop smoking and not to people who have never smoked, and that products containing cannabis or illicit products may have different harm profiles. Certainty: low (for the comparisons with nicotine replacement and with a vape without nicotine; very low against support only or no support). Status: replicated.
lines.population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined randomised trials of nicotine vapes; adverse events 8, 6 and 11 trials (3,107, 909 and 2,801 people) and serious adverse events 10, 11 and 18 trials (4,045, 1,786 and 5,032 people) against nicotine replacement, vapes without nicotine, and support only or no support; follow-up 1 week to about 2 years; Cochrane living review, search to 1 January 2026
lines.comparator: Nicotine replacement therapy; a vape without nicotine; behavioural support only or no support
lines.outcome: Any adverse event and serious adverse event during follow-up of one week or longer (self-report and medical records)
lines.magnitude: Serious adverse events (risk difference; per 100 with comparator vs vape): vs NRT 0.01 (−0.01 to 0.02), 6 vs 7 (5–8), 10 trials, 4,045 participants, moderate; vs non-nicotine vape 0.00 (−0.01 to 0.01), 2 vs 2 (1–3), 11 trials, 1,786, low; vs behavioural support only or no support 0.00 (−0.00 to 0.01), 3 vs 3 (3–4), 18 trials, 5,032, very low. Any adverse event (RR): vs NRT 0.95 (0.72–1.24), 41 vs 39 per 100 (30–51), 8 trials, 3,107, I² 72%, low; vs non-nicotine vape 1.01 (0.95–1.08), 46 vs 46 per 100 (44–50), 6 trials, 909, moderate; vs support only or no support 1.22 (1.00–1.49), 43 vs 52 per 100 (43–64), 11 trials, 2,801, I² 58%, very low. Industry-funded trials left out (Table 2): none to remove against NRT; against a vape without nicotine any adverse event 1.01 (0.95–1.08) and serious events −0.00 (−0.01 to 0.01), unchanged; against support only or no support the review reports no change in reading for serious events, and any adverse event reads 1.26 (0.96–1.66), I² 60%.
lines.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high; the rating is for the comparisons with nicotine replacement and with vapes without nicotine, and the comparison with support only or no support, which the review rates very low, is labelled in the statement rather than allowed to set the claim's rating (METHODS §6.3; the same approach as the all-cause estimate in the methamphetamine mortality claim). Imprecision, two levels: serious adverse events against vapes without nicotine rest on fewer than 100 events (the review's two levels); against nicotine replacement the review took one level for fewer than 300 events, and for any adverse event against nicotine replacement one level for imprecision and one for inconsistency (I² 72%); all reach low. Risk of bias, not rated down for these two comparisons (the review does not downgrade them; for support only or no support it takes levels for unblinded assessment and differential contact). Indirectness, not rated down: regulated vapes supplied in trials, adults, up to about 2 years. Relation insufficient-evidence because the intervals do not exclude a difference of about 2 serious events in 100 against nicotine replacement and the trials were too short and too small to show rare or later harms (METHODS §6.3: no detectable effect needs an interval that excludes meaningful effects). Status replicated for the main finding, serious events, whose pools have I² 0% in all three comparisons; adverse events overall are less consistent (I² 72% and 58%), which the statement shows. Living review: later updates will change the numbers.

lines.q: Is it safe to use a vape to quit smoking?
lines.short: Nobody can say for sure. In quit-smoking trials, serious health problems were about as common with a nicotine vape as with patches or gum: 7 against 6 in 100.
lines.but: Serious problems were few, and the trials lasted about 2 years at most. That's too few and too short to show rare or later harms.
how: A review of trials, searched up to January 2026, looked at adults who smoked and were given regulated nicotine vapes to help them stop. They were followed for 1 week to about 2 years. The review says this doesn't apply to people who never smoked, and that cannabis or illicit vapes may carry different harms.

Serious health problems: 7 in 100 with a vape against 6 in 100 with patches, gum or similar (10 trials, 4,045 people), and 2 in 100 in both groups against a vape without nicotine (11 trials, 1,786 people). Side effects of any kind were about as common too: 39 against 41 in 100, and 46 against 46.

Against counselling only or no help, the evidence is weaker. Serious problems: 3 in 100 in both groups (18 trials, 5,032 people; 10 of them recorded none). Side effects of any kind: 52 in 100 with a vape against 43, though the range includes no difference.

Some trials found more throat or mouth irritation, cough or dry mouth with vapes; others found fewer breathing symptoms. One found more nausea with patches, gum or similar. No trial against those was paid for by the tobacco or vape industry; one or two in each of the others were, and leaving them out didn't change what the review concluded.

lines.statement: In adults who smoked and joined four small randomised trials of oral nicotine pouches (284 people; 7 days to 8 weeks; three of the four trials enrolled people not planning to quit; Cochrane review, search to 13 January 2025, with ten further trials ongoing), the evidence is insufficient to say whether pouches help people stop smoking or cut down, whether compared with continuing to smoke, with a nicotine e-cigarette or with a lower-strength pouch. Compared with continuing to smoke as usual, 1 of 18 people given pouches had quit at week 8 against 0 of 9 (risk ratio 1.58, 95% CI 0.07 to 35.32; one trial, 27 people; very low certainty); among people still smoking, cigarettes per day differed by −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58; 19 people). Compared with a nicotine e-cigarette (the same trial of 45 people, at high risk of bias), 1 of 18 had quit with pouches against 4 of 18 with e-cigarettes (0.25, 0.03 to 2.02; 36 people; low certainty), and people still smoking smoked 5.32 more cigarettes a day with pouches (−2.16 to 12.80; 26 people). Between two pouch strengths (one registry-listed trial), 2 of 15 had quit at the higher strength against 0 of 15 at the lower at week 4 (5.00, 0.26 to 96.13; 30 people). None of these differences can be told from chance. No trial compared pouches with nicotine replacement for quitting (one cross-over trial of 63 people reported side effects only), none followed people beyond 8 weeks, none included people who vape or use other products, and the review found no study of pouch uptake and smoking in the population. No serious adverse events were recorded in any arm of the three trials that reported them (1 to 8 weeks; very low to low certainty); other adverse events were reported in different ways and were mostly mild or uncommon. In the one trial funded by a tobacco company (53 people, about one week), urine and blood measures of smoke exposure were lower with pouches than with continued smoking (a tobacco-specific nitrosamine marker, NNAL, 265 ng/g creatinine lower, 95% CI 180 to 351, from 330; carboxyhaemoglobin 6.7 percentage points lower, 5.1 to 8.3, from 11.3%; very low certainty); it is the only trial in the review to measure those two against continued smoking, and an independent trial of 19 people that measured exhaled carbon monoxide found it lower with pouches, with an interval that included no difference. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
lines.population: Adults who smoked cigarettes and joined four small randomised trials of oral nicotine pouches (284 people; 7 days to 8 weeks; three trials enrolled people not planning to quit); Cochrane review, search to 13 January 2025; ten further trials ongoing
lines.exposure: Oral nicotine pouches given by the trial
lines.comparator: Continuing to smoke as usual; a nicotine e-cigarette; a lower-strength pouch (and, for side effects only, snus and nicotine gum)
lines.outcome: Not smoking at week 8 (week 4 in one trial); cigarettes per day in people still smoking; serious and other adverse events; NNAL and carboxyhaemoglobin after about a week
lines.magnitude: Quitting (RR; events; participants): pouch vs continued smoking at week 8, 1/18 vs 0/9, RR 1.58 (95% CI 0.07–35.32), 1 trial, 27, very low certainty; pouch vs nicotine e-cigarette at week 8, 1/18 vs 4/18, RR 0.25 (0.03–2.02), 1 trial, 36, low certainty (review's table: 222 per 1,000 with e-cigarettes vs 56 per 1,000 with pouches; about 17 fewer in 100 on the point estimate, editors' subtraction); higher vs lower strength at week 4, 2/15 vs 0/15, RR 5.00 (0.26–96.13), 1 trial, 30, not graded. Cigarettes per day among people still smoking: vs continued smoking MD −1.07 (−12.72 to 10.58), 19; vs e-cigarette MD 5.32 (−2.16 to 12.80), 26; higher vs lower strength, log scale MD −0.20 (−0.27 to −0.13), 30. Serious adverse events: none in any arm (3 trials; vs continued smoking 2 trials, 124 participants, very low; vs e-cigarette 1 trial, 26, low; higher vs lower strength 2 trials, 77). Biomarkers vs continued smoking (Rensch 2023, industry-funded, 53 participants): NNAL MD −265.30 ng/g creatinine (−350.64 to −179.96), COHb MD −6.7% (−8.33 to −5.07); very low.
lines.reasoning: Randomised evidence, starting high, read through a Cochrane systematic review that found no meta-analysis worth pooling (AMSTAR 2: high confidence, on the study card). Risk of bias, two levels: none of the four trials was at low risk and three were high, with unblinded arms and unequal interventions in the two trials that matter for quitting; the comparison with continued smoking rests on one trial at high risk of bias (the review's two levels). Indirectness, one level: quitting was measured at 4 to 8 weeks, not the 6 months that the claim's question needs, three of the four trials enrolled people not planning to quit, and no trial included people who vape or use other products. Imprecision, two levels: five people had quit across all comparisons, and the risk ratios' intervals run from 0.03 to 96. Inconsistency does not arise (single trials). Publication bias, not rated down but recorded: ten further trials are ongoing and industry reports were not searched. The total of five levels is more than the three available, so the rating is very low; it is not changed by the biomarker result, which is a separate outcome from one tobacco-industry trial (very low), with no independent trial to set beside it. Relation insufficient-evidence (METHODS §6.1). Status single study: the comparison with continued smoking and the comparison with e-cigarettes come from the same trial of 45 people, the higher-against-lower-strength comparison from a registry record of one trial, and the review's plain language summary speaks of two studies behind those comparisons when both come from one trial.

lines.q: Do nicotine pouches help people stop smoking?
lines.short: Nobody knows yet. Four small trials, with 284 people over 8 weeks at most, couldn't tell whether pouches help people quit or cut down.
lines.but: Three of the four trials took people who weren't planning to quit. None compared pouches with patches or gum for quitting.
how: A review of trials, searched up to January 2025, found only four small ones in adults who smoked: 284 people, followed for 7 days to 8 weeks. Ten more trials are under way.

In one trial of 45 people, 1 of 18 given pouches had quit at week 8. That compares with 0 of 9 who kept smoking as usual and 4 of 18 given a nicotine vape. None of these gaps, or those in cigarettes a day, can be told from chance, and the trial had serious design flaws.
No serious health problems were recorded in the three trials that reported them, over 1 to 8 weeks. Other side effects were reported in different ways and were mostly mild or uncommon.

A trial paid for by a tobacco company tested 53 people after about a week. Those on pouches had less carbon monoxide in blood, and less of a tobacco chemical in urine, than those who kept smoking. No other trial measured these.

lines.statement: In adults who smoked or had smoked cigarettes, vaping as the only product, compared with smoking cigarettes only, is associated with much lower levels of tobacco-specific nitrosamines, carbon monoxide and most other smoke chemicals in urine, breath and blood, but not with a clear fall in nicotine itself, and the levels stay above those of people who use no tobacco or nicotine; in the national survey, and in a smaller cross-sectional comparison, people who both vaped and smoked did not show the lower levels. The main data are from the first wave (2013–2014) of the US PATH survey (Goniewicz et al., 2018; 247 adults who only vaped, 93% of whom had smoked before, against 2,411 who only smoked; funded by the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Food and Drug Administration's Center for Tobacco Products, whose staff took part in the analysis and in preparing and approving the manuscript; one author reports advisory fees from Johnson & Johnson and grant support from Pfizer, and another an honorarium from Pfizer and unpaid contact with Juul Labs staff): the nitrosamine metabolite NNAL was 4.887 against 203.5 pg/mg creatinine (about 98% lower), the acrylonitrile marker 3.959 against 123.9 ng/mg (97% lower), the acrolein marker 108.0 against 271.5 (60% lower) and cadmium 0.193 against 0.277 (30% lower), while most other metals and the markers for toluene, benzene and carbon disulfide did not differ. Total nicotine equivalents were 2.000 against 27.90 nmol/mg (about 93% lower), but only 59% of the people who only vaped (161 people, as printed) reported using nicotine-containing e-cigarettes; in the UK review's five pooled analyses of people who vaped against people who smoked at least weekly, nicotine and its metabolites did not differ significantly, and the National Academies judged nicotine intake in experienced adults who vape comparable to that from cigarettes (the committee's judgment: substantial evidence). Switching and confinement studies point the same way for the other chemicals. A 2023 systematic review of nine studies (1,299 adults who smoked, one week to 8 months, eight at high risk of bias; funded by an Oxford University grant, Cancer Research UK and infrastructure funding from the National Institute for Health Research; authors' declarations include consultancy and research funding from Pfizer and consultancy to Johnson & Johnson Japan on nicotine replacement; two included studies, Cravo 2016 and Morris 2022, are marked industry funded) found exhaled carbon monoxide 9.57 ppm lower with vaping only than with smoking only (95% CI −17.30 to −1.83; 3 studies) and 12 of 13 other biomarkers lower with none higher, those rows resting on the two industry-funded studies. The UK review (2022; commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; no declarations of interest on the pages read; its authors say many pooled findings came from tobacco industry-funded trials in confinement lasting up to 7 days) pooled studies of people who vaped against people who smoked and found lower NNAL (58%), NNN (90%), the acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA (71%), the acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA (94%) and the butadiene metabolite MHBMA (83%), and lower blood carboxyhaemoglobin in two analyses.
