The National Academies (2018; contract with the Food and Drug Administration; its Reviewers page lists one reviewer employed by British American Tobacco Research and Development Centre; its online table of study sponsors was not read) judged it conclusive that completely substituting e-cigarettes for cigarettes reduces exposure to numerous toxicants and carcinogens. The publicly funded survey and the industry-funded trials point the same way. Against people who use no tobacco or nicotine, people who only vaped had higher levels in the survey (NNAL 4.887 against 0.921 pg/mg; also lead, cadmium, a pyrene marker and the acrylonitrile marker), and the UK review found significantly higher nitrosamines in three cross-sectional analyses, no significant difference for most volatile compounds (the acrylonitrile metabolite excepted, over three times higher in one study), higher nicotine in four analyses and mixed results for metals; its authors say cross-sectional data make it hard to separate exposure from vaping from earlier smoking, and that a trial and a cross-over study suggest nitrosamine metabolites might fall to the levels of people who use no nicotine. In the one small study with an abstinent group, exhaled carbon monoxide at 12 weeks was 1 ppm in both the vaping group (16 people) and the abstinent group (12). Against people who both vaped and smoked, the survey's dual group had higher levels than people who only smoked (total nicotine equivalents 43.70 against 27.90 nmol/mg; NNAL 262.6 against 203.5 pg/mg) at similar numbers of cigarettes a day (15.1 against 15.4), and the National Academies describe a smaller cross-sectional comparison (181 people) in which nitrosamine and volatile-compound metabolites in people who did both were similar to those in people who only smoked; in the switching studies exhaled carbon monoxide was 1.91 ppm lower with both than with smoking only (95% CI −3.38 to −0.45) and 4.40 ppm lower with vaping only than with both (−12.04 to 3.24, an interval that includes no difference). Against another form (product content, not body levels), the National Academies report tobacco-specific nitrosamines in e-liquids and aerosol at low levels, typically similar to those in pharmaceutical nicotine products. Markers of potential harm after switching are less settled: in the UK review, acute vaping and acute smoking each lowered the arteries' flow-mediated dilation in the short term, one trial found it improved after four weeks of switching, and C-reactive protein was lower than in people who smoke in pooled cross-sectional data but not in controlled studies; its authors draw only limited conclusions. What this does not show: these are levels of chemicals, not illness; the UK review could not summarise exposure beyond 12 months and says the degree of any residual risk remains unclear; most people who vaped had smoked for years, so earlier smoking may contribute to some markers; the survey's devices were early-generation and its group of people who only vaped was small; nickel, chromium and flavoring compounds were not measured there; and people who vape and have never smoked are almost absent from these data. Certainty: low. Status: replicated for the lower nitrosamine, carbon monoxide and volatile-compound levels (the survey, the switching studies and the reviews overlap in part and are not counted as separate replications); the nicotine and dual-use comparisons are mixed.
lines.population: Adults who smoked cigarettes or had smoked them: US adults in the first wave (2013–2014) of the national PATH survey (247 who only vaped, 93% of them had smoked before; 2,411 who only smoked; 792 who did both; 1,655 who had never used tobacco), adults in nine short switching and confinement studies (1,299 people; Greece, Italy, Poland, the UK and the US; one week to 8 months), and the studies pooled by the UK review (2022; 24 to 60 studies per chemical, follow-up from one session to 12 months) and described by the National Academies (2018); people who vape and have never smoked are almost absent
lines.exposure: Vaping (e-cigarettes) as the only product: in the survey, self-reported current use every day or some days and no other tobacco (59% of the group reported nicotine-containing e-cigarettes, as printed); in the switching and confinement studies, being given or switching to an e-cigarette
lines.comparator: Smoking cigarettes only (main comparison); doing both (vaping and smoking); using no tobacco or nicotine (the survey's never-used group; abstainers in one small study)
lines.outcome: Levels of nicotine, tobacco-specific nitrosamines (NNAL), carbon monoxide and other smoke chemicals (volatile compounds, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, metals) measured in urine, breath and blood; short-term markers of potential harm (inflammation, oxidative stress, flow-mediated dilation, heart rate, blood pressure) after switching. These are measures of what reaches the body, not of disease.
lines.magnitude: Against people who only smoke (levels in urine unless stated; absolute values before relative). National survey (PATH, 2013–2014; 247 people who only vaped against 2,411 who only smoked; geometric means per mg creatinine): total nicotine equivalents 2.000 (95% CI 1.100–3.500) against 27.90 (23.80–32.70) nmol, about 93% lower; NNAL 4.887 (3.817–6.257) against 203.5 (181.7–227.9) pg, about 98% lower; acrylonitrile marker 3.959 (3.002–5.219) against 123.9 (109.9–139.7) ng, 97% lower; acrolein marker 108.0 (95.93–121.6) against 271.5 (255.1–289.0) ng, 60% lower; acrylamide marker 56.05 against 136.4 ng, 59% lower; naphthalene marker 62% and pyrene marker 47% lower; cadmium 0.193 against 0.277 ng, 30% lower; nearly all other metals and the toluene, benzene and carbon disulfide markers similar (percentages recomputed by the editors from the printed means, within one point of the text). 2023 systematic review (nine studies, 1,299 adults, one week to 8 months): exhaled carbon monoxide, vaping only against smoking only −9.57 ppm (−17.30 to −1.83; 3 studies); 12 of 13 other biomarkers lower with vaping only, none higher, one (NNN) not different. UK review (McNeill et al., 2022), pooled analyses of people who vaped against people who smoked: NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94% and NNN 90% lower (5 analyses); 3-HPMA 71%, CNEMA 94% and MHBMA 83% lower (15 analyses; formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive); blood carboxyhaemoglobin significantly lower (2 analyses); nicotine and its metabolites not significantly different (5 analyses, against people who smoked at least weekly). Against people who use no tobacco or nicotine: survey, never-used group (1,655 people) against people who only vaped: NNAL 0.921 (0.819–1.035) against 4.887 pg (81% lower), lead 0.351 against 0.432 ng, cadmium 0.149 against 0.193 ng, pyrene marker 0.128 against 0.161 ng, acrylonitrile marker 1.315 against 3.959 ng (about 66% lower); all major nicotine metabolites, all nitrosamines, 4 metals, 1 polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon and 4 volatile-compound markers were higher in the group that only vaped. UK review: nitrosamines significantly higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses; nicotine significantly higher in 4; volatile compounds not different in 10 analyses except CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); metals mixed, mostly higher; other toxicants (9 studies, not pooled) higher. One study with an abstinent group: exhaled carbon monoxide at 12 weeks 1 ppm (SD 1) in 16 people who vaped and in 12 who abstained. Against people who both vaped and smoked: survey, both group (792 people) against smoking only: total nicotine equivalents 43.70 (39.80–48.10) against 27.90 nmol; NNAL 262.6 (240.0–287.3) against 203.5 pg; the smoking-only group was lower by 15% for the pyrene marker, 10% for the acrolein marker and 15% for the acrylonitrile marker; lead and cadmium did not differ; cigarettes a day 15.1 against 15.4. Switching studies: exhaled carbon monoxide, vaping only against both −4.40 ppm (−12.04 to 3.24; 2 studies); both against smoking only −1.91 ppm (−3.38 to −0.45; 2 studies); of 25 biomarkers, 12 lower with vaping only, 5 lower with both (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon metabolites, one study of 22 people) and 8 not different or inconsistent. Markers of potential harm (UK review): flow-mediated dilation lowered in the short term by both acute vaping and acute smoking and improved by 4 weeks of switching in one randomized trial; C-reactive protein lower than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine in pooled cross-sectional data (3 studies), not confirmed in controlled or longitudinal studies; LDL cholesterol no difference; blood pressure lower than in people who smoke and similar to people who use no nicotine in pooled cross-sectional analyses of people who had vaped for at least 3 months or a year; heart rate lower than in people who smoke when the groups were mutually exclusive; pulse wave velocity may fall after a sustained switch (longest follow-up 4 months). Follow-up: a single session to 7 days (acute) or 8 days to 12 months in the UK review; one week to 8 months in the 2023 review; the survey is a single time point.
lines.reasoning: Observational evidence (a cross-sectional survey; non-randomised and some randomized short studies behind the reviews) starts low. Downgraded once for risk of bias; not downgraded again for the same problem in another domain. Upgraded once for a large effect, applied to evidence already rated down for risk of bias: a strict reading, without the upgrade, gives very low, and the gap between the two is the chance that the lower levels are partly produced by who chooses to vape and how they are classified, which the direction of the main biases (toward smaller differences) and the consistency across a survey, short switching studies and four syntheses argue against but do not exclude. The rating applies to the headline contrast only (people who only vaped against people who only smoked, for nitrosamines, carbon monoxide and volatile compounds). The nicotine comparison, the comparison of people who vape and smoke, the metals, the product-content comparison with pharmaceutical nicotine products and the markers of potential harm after switching are less certain and, taken alone, would be rated very low. The reviews' graded judgments (conclusive, substantial, moderate) are their authors' judgments from a different starting point and are reported, not adopted. Funding is set out in the statement: the industry-funded trials are read beside the publicly funded survey and neither is dropped. Overlap: the 2023 review, the UK pooled analyses and the National Academies chapters share primary studies and are not independent replications; the survey is independent of them. Rated as worded: an association in levels of chemicals, which is not a claim about disease.

lines.q: Does vaping put fewer toxic chemicals in your body than smoking?
lines.short: Yes, much less of most. But not clearly less nicotine. In a US survey, people who only vaped had about 98% less of one cancer-linked chemical than people who only smoked.
lines.but: These are chemical levels, not illness. And people who both vaped and smoked didn't have the lower levels.
how: A US survey in 2013 and 2014 compared 247 adults who only vaped (93 in 100 had smoked before) with 2,411 who only smoked. Those who only vaped had about 98% less of a cancer-linked tobacco chemical in their urine and 30% to 97% less of some others. Most metals and a few other chemicals didn't differ.

Short studies where people switched to vaping found the same for carbon monoxide and most other chemicals. So did reviews for the UK in 2022 and by a US expert panel in 2018. Some of those studies were paid for by tobacco companies, but the survey, paid for with public money, agrees.

In the survey, nicotine was 93% lower, but only 59 in 100 of those who only vaped said their vapes had nicotine. In the UK review's pooled studies, nicotine didn't clearly differ. The US panel judged that adults used to vaping take in about as much as from cigarettes.

People who only vaped still had more of some chemicals than people who used no tobacco or nicotine. In the survey, people who both vaped and smoked had as much as people who only smoked, or more, at about the same number of cigarettes a day. Most who vaped had smoked for years, and no study looked past about a year.

lines.statement: In US adults followed for up to about four years in the national PATH cohort, and in three reviews commissioned by governments, the evidence is insufficient to say whether vaping, compared with using neither cigarettes nor e-cigarettes, changes the risk of heart disease, stroke or long-term lung disease, and the sources read give no cancer rates for people who vape; this is not evidence that vaping has no effect. The cohort found no detectable difference in newly reported heart disease or stroke between people who only vaped and people who used neither, with wide intervals and few events, and a higher rate of newly reported lung conditions in people who had used e-cigarettes, which smoking history may explain. Heart (Berlowitz et al., 2022, a research letter; PATH Waves 1 to 5, 2013–2019; funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, the Food and Drug Administration's Center for Tobacco Products and the American Lung Association; one author reports grants from Johnson & Johnson): of 24,027 adults with no heart disease at the start, 1,487 reported a new diagnosis of heart disease or stroke over up to four years: 764 of 14,832 who used neither product, 41 of 822 who only vaped, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both (counts, not rates: the groups differ in age and follow-up; the age-adjusted rates as printed were, in that order, 8.0, 9.7, 14.8 and 17.1 per 1,000 person-years, which the editors could not reproduce from the counts). After adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, family history, marijuana use, pack-years and other tobacco, the hazard ratio against using neither was 1.00 (95% CI 0.69–1.45) for people who only vaped, 1.53 (1.30–1.79) for people who only smoked and 1.54 (1.21–1.96) for people who did both; for heart attack, heart failure or stroke alone (15 events among people who only vaped) 1.35 (0.75–2.42), 2.20 (1.73–2.81) and 2.08 (1.40–3.09). Against people who only smoked the ratio was 0.66 (0.46–0.94) for people who only vaped (0.61, 0.34–1.09, for the narrower outcome) and 1.01 (0.81–1.26) for people who did both (0.94, 0.65–1.36). The outcomes were self-reported and not adjudicated; the comparison group included people who had stopped smoking; and people who only vaped had more pack-years than that group (mean 11.0 against 4.2, with spreads several times the means), so past smoking may account for part of a difference or hide one. Lungs (Xie et al., 2020; PATH Waves 1 to 4, 2013–2018; same funders; one author reports grants from Ethicon, a Johnson & Johnson subsidiary, and other authors report federal grants and, for one, personal fees from several pharmaceutical companies): of 21,618 adults with no respiratory condition at the start, 1,460 (6.8%) reported a new diagnosis of asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis. After adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, region, smoking history (never; former by years since quitting; current by pack-years), other tobacco, other drug use, body mass index and chronic conditions, the adjusted rate was 26.06 against 20.41 per 1,000 person-years (about 2.6 against 2.0 in 100 a year, editors' conversion) in people who had ever used e-cigarettes at the start against people who had not (rate ratio 1.28, 1.10–1.48), with the same ratio for former use (1.28), which includes people who had tried 1 or 2 puffs, and a similar one for current use (1.31, 1.08–1.59); by condition, COPD 1.62, emphysema 1.54, chronic bronchitis 1.33 and asthma 1.24 (1.01–1.53). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone the ratios were much larger (2.14 for any condition, 5.03 for COPD), which shows how much depends on handling past smoking; use was recorded at the first wave only; 401 people (16.0% of those currently vaping) had never smoked cigarettes, so most had smoked; and the ratio was 1.20 (0.99–1.45) among people with no chronic condition at the start. Residual confounding by how much people smoked and when they stopped is likely, and the authors say causality cannot be established. The reviews. The National Academies (2018; contract with the Food and Drug Administration; its Reviewers page lists one reviewer employed by British American Tobacco Research and Development Centre; its online table of study sponsors was not read) found no available evidence whether e-cigarette use is associated with coronary heart disease, stroke or peripheral artery disease, none whether e-cigarettes cause respiratory disease, none on intermediate cancer endpoints and none on long-term illness or death in people who both vape and smoke; it judged the evidence substantial for a short-term rise in heart rate and moderate for a rise in diastolic blood pressure after nicotine intake, moderate for more cough and wheeze, and for an association with more asthma attacks, in adolescents who vape (four cross-sectional, self-reported studies), limited for better lung function or fewer COPD flare-ups in adults with asthma or COPD who switched from smoking (small studies), and substantial for fewer short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems when people switched completely from smoking (mostly small studies). The UK review (2022; commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; search to July 2021; no declarations of interest on the pages read) said that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular outcomes and that the extent of cardiovascular risk remains uncertain, rated the evidence from lung tests insufficient either way and limited for fewer COPD flare-ups in adults who switch completely (two reports on one group of patients), and presented no cancer incidence data; the review questions it lists concern markers linked to risk and people with existing conditions, so the pages read do not show a search for new disease in the general population (editors' reading; the Methods are in a PDF not read). The Australian review (Banks et al., 2023; Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council; no relevant disclosures; searches to July 2020, with major reviews to December 2021) rated clinical cardiovascular outcomes and invasive cancer as no available evidence and asthma, bronchitis and COPD as insufficient evidence in people who smoke and no available evidence in people who do not, with certainty low or very low, and judged the direct effect on clinical disease largely unknown; it also judged it conclusive that vaping products cause an acute lung injury (EVALI), largely with THC-containing products, though in the largest study 14% of cases reported only nicotine products. The heart analysis appeared after all three reviews' searches ended; the lung analysis appeared after the Australian top-up search and neither is named in the Australian paper's reference list or on the UK pages read; a published critique (Mendelsohn et al., 2022, a commentary on the 2022 report to the Australian Department of Health on which the Australian review is based; no funding statement; two of its four authors were or are board members of the Australian Tobacco Harm Reduction Association, a registered health promotion charity that accepted unconditional seed funding from the vape retail industry until March 2019, and both state they have never received payments from electronic cigarette or tobacco companies; one is the author of a book titled Stop Smoking Start Vaping; the other two declare no interests; the full statement is in the anchor) argues that the review should have compared vaping with continuing to smoke, weighed net effects on the population and judged evidence on quitting by the same standard as evidence on starting to smoke, and that the 14% of lung-injury cases reporting only nicotine products do not show a link with nicotine, because many patients who denied vaping THC were later found to have done so; it cites no study of how often heart disease, lung disease or cancer occur in people who vape, only short-term measures after switching (mostly from studies that share authors) and a modelled cancer estimate, so it and the review disagree on the comparison and on which kinds of evidence count, not on disease rates, which neither measured. Not known: whether vaping causes any heart disease, lung disease or cancer in people who have never smoked, over more than four years or with current devices; whether the higher rate of lung conditions reflects vaping or past smoking; and cancer rates. Certainty: very low. Status: single study (two analyses of one cohort, which share data and some authors and are not independent replications).
lines.population: US adults in the national PATH cohort followed from 2013–2014 for up to about four years: 24,027 with no heart disease or stroke at the start (heart analysis, Waves 1 to 5) and 21,618 with no asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis at the start (lung analysis, Waves 1 to 4); most of the people who vaped had smoked (in the lung analysis 16.0% of those currently vaping had never smoked cigarettes); and the reviews of the wider literature by the National Academies (2018), the UK government (2022; search to July 2021) and the Australian government (2023; studies to July 2020, major reviews to December 2021)
lines.exposure: Vaping (e-cigarette use): current use of any frequency, updated at each wave (heart analysis), or ever, former or current use at the first wave only (lung analysis), with or without smoking
lines.comparator: People who used neither cigarettes nor e-cigarettes (the heart analysis's reference group, which includes people who had stopped smoking); people who only smoked cigarettes; people who both vaped and smoked; in the lung analysis, people who had never used an e-cigarette (including people who smoked)
lines.outcome: Newly reported, self-reported diagnoses of heart disease or stroke (heart analysis) and of asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis (lung analysis) over up to about four years; and what three reviews concluded about heart disease, lung disease and cancer
lines.magnitude: Absolute counts and rates before ratios. Heart (Berlowitz et al., 2022; PATH Waves 1 to 5; 24,027 adults with no heart disease at the start; up to 4 years): new self-reported diagnosis of heart disease or stroke in 764 of 14,832 people who used neither product, 41 of 822 who only vaped, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both (counts only; the groups differ in age and follow-up); age-adjusted rates as printed per 1,000 person-years 8.0, 9.7, 14.8 and 17.1 in that order (not reproducible from the counts). Hazard ratios against using neither, fully adjusted: only vaping 1.00 (0.69–1.45), only smoking 1.53 (1.30–1.79), both 1.54 (1.21–1.96); for heart attack, heart failure or stroke (519 cases, 15 among people who only vaped) 1.35 (0.75–2.42), 2.20 (1.73–2.81) and 2.08 (1.40–3.09). Against people who only smoked: only vaping 0.66 (0.46–0.94) and 0.61 (0.34–1.09); both 1.01 (0.81–1.26) and 0.94 (0.65–1.36). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone, only vaping against neither 1.16 (0.82–1.66) and 1.55 (0.87–2.76). Lungs (Xie et al., 2020; PATH Waves 1 to 4; 21,618 adults with no respiratory condition at the start; up to about 4 years): 1,460 (6.8%) with at least one new diagnosis (asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948 new diagnoses); adjusted rate per 1,000 person-years for any condition: never used 20.41 (18.65–22.17), ever 26.06 (22.63–29.49), former 26.12, current 26.68 (21.83–31.52) (about 2.0 against 2.6–2.7 in 100 a year, editors' conversion); for single conditions, never against ever: COPD 6.48 against 10.49, emphysema 3.74 against 5.76, chronic bronchitis 12.18 against 16.23, asthma 10.73 against 13.31. Rate ratios against never use (fully adjusted, ever / former / current): any condition 1.28 (1.10–1.48) / 1.28 (1.09–1.51) / 1.31 (1.08–1.59); chronic bronchitis 1.33 / 1.31 / 1.33; emphysema 1.54 / 1.42 / 1.69; COPD 1.62 / 1.66 / 1.57; asthma 1.24 (1.01–1.53) / 1.19 (0.95–1.50) / 1.32 (1.01–1.72). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone the ratios for ever use were 2.14 (any condition), 4.02 (emphysema) and 5.03 (COPD). Among people with good or better self-rated health (18,649): former 1.21 (1.00–1.47), current 1.43 (1.14–1.80); among people with no chronic condition at baseline (14,865): ever 1.20 (0.99–1.45), former 1.11 (0.90–1.37), current 1.40 (1.09–1.79). Reviews (the authors' own gradings): National Academies 2018 conclusions 9-1 (clinical cardiovascular outcomes, no available evidence), 11-1 (respiratory disease, no available evidence), 10-1 (intermediate cancer endpoints, no available evidence), 18-3 (long-term illness or death in people who vape and smoke, no available evidence), 11-4 (cough and wheeze in adolescents, moderate), 11-2 and 11-3 (adults with asthma or COPD who switch, limited); UK review 2022: clinical cardiovascular outcomes still no available evidence, cardiovascular risk uncertain, lung tests insufficient, no cancer incidence data; Australian review 2023: clinical cardiovascular outcomes and invasive cancer no available evidence, asthma, bronchitis and COPD insufficient in people who smoke and no available evidence in people who do not, certainty low or very low, EVALI conclusive (14% of cases in the largest study reported only nicotine products, 2% only non-nicotine products). Follow-up: up to 4 years in both cohort analyses; the reviews' evidence mostly concerns short-term effects.
lines.reasoning: Observational cohorts start low. Downgraded once for risk of bias (both analyses rated high on ROBINS-E) and once for imprecision (few events in people who only vaped), which reaches the floor, very low. Rated as worded: the claim is that the evidence is insufficient to say whether vaping changes the risk of heart or lung disease, not that vaping has no effect; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The three reviews' judgments (no available evidence, insufficient evidence, low or very low certainty) are their authors' judgments and are reported, not adopted. Overlap: the heart and lung analyses are two analyses of one cohort that share data and some authors, so they are not independent replications; the reviews overlap in the studies they draw on. The acute lung injury outbreak (EVALI) is outside the rating: the Australian review judged it conclusive, largely with THC-containing products. A published critique of the Australian review (Mendelsohn et al., 2022) disputes its comparison group and standards of evidence but brings no data on disease rates, so it changes no rating. Funding is set out in the statement: no tobacco or vape industry funding is declared for the cohort analyses or the reviews read; the pharmaceutical and device-company ties of some authors are listed as printed, and the sponsors of the studies in the National Academies report are in an online table that was not read.

lines.q: Does vaping cause heart or lung disease?
lines.short: Nobody can say yet. A big US study found no clear rise in heart disease in people who only vaped, and more lung problems that past smoking may explain.
lines.but: It's one study, of illnesses people reported themselves, over 4 years at most. Only 41 people who only vaped got heart disease, too few to be sure either way.
how: The study followed about 24,000 US adults for up to 4 years. New heart disease or stroke was reported by 41 of 822 who only vaped, 764 of 14,832 who used neither, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both. The groups differed in age and time followed, so these counts aren't rates.

Allowing for age, health and past smoking, people who only vaped didn't clearly differ from people who used neither, while those who smoked, or smoked and vaped, had about 1.5 times the rate. But the group who used neither included people who had quit smoking, and those who only vaped had smoked more in the past.

In the same study, new lung conditions such as asthma or COPD came to about 2.6 in 100 people a year among those who had ever vaped, against 2.0 among those who never had. Most who vaped had smoked, and without allowing for past smoking the gap looked far bigger. The authors say this can't show that vaping caused it.

Three reviews were done for the US, UK and Australian governments. They found no evidence, or too little, on heart attack, stroke, long-term lung disease or cancer from vaping. The Australian one judged that vapes did cause a lung injury outbreak (EVALI), mostly vapes with THC.

lines.statement: In US adults who used only e-cigarettes every day (156 people), compared with adults who smoked only cigarettes every day (3,430), in the first wave (2013–2014) of the national PATH survey, the e-cigarette group said yes less often to each of four dependence questions: self-rated dependence 77.2% against 94.0%, strong cravings 72.8% against 86.9%, difficulty keeping from using where it was prohibited 5.6% against 28.6%, and feeling they really needed to use 71.5% against 88.5% (adjusted odds ratios for the cigarette group 2.85 to 6.92, every interval excluding 1); they also waited longer after waking before first use (adjusted geometric mean 29.2 against 20.0 minutes) (Liu et al., 2017). Dependence symptoms were therefore common among adults who only vaped every day, and less common than among adults who only smoked every day. Other surveys, read only as the National Academies describe them, point the same way (a 2012–2013 US telephone survey of 124 against 3,963 adults; a second analysis of the same PATH wave; a voluntary web survey of 3,609 people who vaped daily and recalled their earlier smoking), as do 2021 surveys of young people in England (52.5% of 16–19-year-olds who vaped rated themselves a little or very dependent, against 83% of those who smoked; McNeill et al., 2022). The National Academies judged the evidence that vaping results in dependence symptoms substantial, that the risk and severity are lower than for cigarettes moderate, and that product features (device type, nicotine concentration, flavouring, brand) are an important determinant moderate (the committee's judgments; the UK review restates them); the Australian review judged the evidence in people who smoke limited and in people who do not smoke substantial (Banks et al., 2023). Where product features were measured, in a voluntary web survey, higher dependence scores went with larger, more advanced devices and with a higher nicotine concentration of the liquid. These are one-time surveys with no follow-up. Nearly all of the e-cigarette group (92.9%) had smoked before and earlier smoking was not adjusted for; the people who keep vaping daily are a small selected share of those who try it; one item (difficulty refraining where use is prohibited) is a less valid indicator for e-cigarettes; there is no agreed scale for comparing the two; the surveys date from 2012–2014 and cannot speak to newer products such as nicotine-salt liquids and disposables, which the UK and Australian reviews describe as little studied; and nothing read follows dependence over time or compares dependence on vaping with dependence on smoking in people who have never smoked. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Adults in the United States who used only e-cigarettes, or only cigarettes, every day (PATH Wave 1, 2013–2014); young people aged 11 to 19 in England (2021 surveys); other adult surveys as described by the National Academies
lines.outcome: Dependence symptoms (self-rated dependence, strong cravings, difficulty keeping from using where prohibited, feeling a need to use, time to first use after waking) and dependence index scores
lines.magnitude: Daily e-cigarette-only (n = 156) vs daily cigarette-only (n = 3,430), PATH Wave 1, weighted: self-rated dependence 77.2% vs 94.0% (adjusted odds ratio for the cigarette group 6.92, 95% CL 4.46–10.73); strong cravings 72.8% vs 86.9% (2.85, 1.92–4.23); difficulty keeping from using where prohibited 5.6% vs 28.6% (6.39, 2.85–14.32); felt they really needed to use 71.5% vs 88.5% (3.89, 2.36–6.40); time to first use after waking, adjusted geometric mean 29.16 (24.39–34.87) vs 20.03 (18.66–21.49) minutes (editors' calculation: ratio 1.46). As described by the National Academies: US National Adult Tobacco Survey 2012–2013, daily e-cigarette-only n = 124 vs cigarette-only n = 3,963, every symptom less common in the e-cigarette group (for example use within 30 minutes of waking 46.1%, 35.1–57.4); PATH Wave 1 item-response index, e-cigarette-only (n = 437) 1.37 SD units below cigarette-only (n = 8,689); web survey of 3,609 people who vaped daily, index 8.1 vs 14.5 for recalled smoking. England 2021, 16–19-year-olds: rated themselves a little or very dependent 52.5% of those who vaped vs 83% of those who smoked (McNeill et al., 2022).
lines.reasoning: Observational (cross-sectional survey) evidence starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. The National Academies rate the lower-dependence comparison moderate and the dependence finding substantial, and the UK review repeats those ratings; these are the authors' judgments over mixed study types, not a GRADE rating, and overlapping reports and the two PATH analyses are counted once. Status replicated rests on independent datasets (US telephone survey, PATH, a web survey, English youth surveys) that agree on direction, three of them known here only through the reviews.

lines.q: Is vaping as addictive as smoking?
lines.short: Less, it seems, but still common. In a US survey, 77 in 100 adults who only vaped daily said they felt dependent, against 94 in 100 who only smoked daily.
lines.but: Nearly all who vaped had smoked before. And the survey is from 2013 to 2014, before disposables and newer liquids were common.
how: A US survey in 2013 and 2014 compared 156 adults who only vaped daily with 3,430 who only smoked daily. Fewer who vaped said they had strong cravings (73 against 87 in 100) or found it hard to go without where it was banned (6 against 29 in 100).

They also waited longer after waking to first use it: about 29 minutes against 20, on average. The question about places where it's banned fits vaping less well. And there's no agreed way to compare the two.

Other US surveys pointed the same way, and so did surveys of young people in England in 2021. There, about half of 16- to 19-year-olds who vaped felt a little or very dependent, against 83 in 100 who smoked. In one web survey, bigger, more advanced vapes and liquids with more nicotine went with higher dependence scores.

A US expert panel judged that vaping can lead to signs of dependence, and, less firmly, that the risk is lower than with smoking. An Australian review was surer of this for people who don't smoke than for those who do. Each survey was a one-time look, and nobody followed people over time.

lines.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether the vapour breathed out by people who vape harms the health of people nearby: no study read measured disease, or early markers of disease, in people exposed to it, so what is known is exposure. Compared with the same air before or without vaping, chamber, home and convention studies found higher airborne nicotine and fine particles than background in every study that measured them, by the National Academies' account (one home study's median fine-particle level matched a non-vaping home although it rose in real time during vaping; in a chamber with five people vaping, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 µg/m3 against undetectable and fine particles (PM2.5) 152 against 32.4 µg/m3; at a vaping convention an estimated 24-hour average PM10 of 1,800 µg/m3, 12 times the US 24-hour standard), rising with the number of people vaping; in homes, cotinine (a breakdown product of nicotine) in saliva and urine was higher in 5 non-smoking people living with someone who vaped than in people in control homes; and in six biomarker studies summarised by the UK review, short exposures produced no detectable change in nicotine, volatile organic compounds or tobacco-specific nitrosamines, while longer exposure during heavy sustained vaping raised nicotine or breakdown products of toxicants. Against second-hand cigarette smoke, levels were lower in the four studies that compared them (airborne nicotine 3.32 against 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 152 against 819 µg/m3 in one chamber; 0.13 against 0.74 µg/m3 airborne nicotine in homes), which the National Academies rated moderate evidence while adding that the health effects of the lower exposures are unknown and that children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may be at special risk; a modelling study found a high-emitting device in a bar scenario exceeding acute reference levels for formaldehyde and acrolein, with estimated health loss in some scenarios comparable to second-hand smoke. A Dutch risk assessment (Visser et al., 2019) measured the first breath of 17 volunteers after one puff (nicotine in all but one, propylene glycol in 4, tobacco-specific nitrosamines in the 9 tested, glycerol in none) and modelled worst-case scenarios: the margins between modelled exposure and the level at which effects are expected were small for nicotine's effect on heart rate and blood pressure in a car (2.1), for propylene glycol irritation (17), and below the authors' threshold for nitrosamines and tumour risk in both a car and an office (521 and 2,297 against 10,000); nothing was measured in a room, a car or a person nearby, and the authors call the effects relatively mild even in the extreme scenario. The Australian review rated the rise in indoor particulate matter conclusive and airborne nicotine limited, and the evidence that these are at hazardous levels insufficient (Banks et al., 2023). The studies were single sessions of minutes to hours or one-off home measurements, in small groups, and mostly published between 2014 and 2017; no study followed people nearby for weeks or years. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated (the exposure findings).
lines.population: People who do not vape who are near someone vaping (volunteers in chambers and rooms, people living with someone who vapes, people at vaping conventions); 17 adults who vaped daily whose breath was measured (Netherlands)
lines.exposure: Breathing air in which someone has vaped (second-hand vapour)
lines.comparator: The same air without vaping (background), and, in four studies, air with cigarette smoke
lines.outcome: Health effects in people nearby (not measured in any study read); exposure measures: airborne nicotine, fine particles and other chemicals, and nicotine biomarkers
lines.magnitude: Health effects in people nearby: not measured in any study read. Exposure, as the National Academies describe the studies (vaping against baseline or control): chamber with 5 people vaping, one-hour air nicotine 3.32 (SD 2.49) vs undetectable µg/m3 and PM2.5 152 (86.8) vs 32.4 µg/m3; 9 volunteers for 2 hours in a café-like room, PM2.5 197 vs 6 µg/m3 and nicotine 2.2 vs below 0.04 µg/m3; 37 volunteers over 4 hours, nicotine 0.38 to 2.83 µg/m3 (several-fold below workplace limits); homes of people living with someone vaping more than 2 hours a day vs control homes, median air nicotine 0.11 vs 0.01 µg/m3, salivary cotinine 0.24 vs 0.05 ng/mL, urinary cotinine 2.64 vs 0.72 ng/mL; convention, estimated 24-hour PM10 1,800 µg/m3. Against second-hand cigarette smoke: one chamber, airborne nicotine 3.32 vs 31.60 µg/m3 and PM2.5 151.7 vs 819.3 µg/m3 (stated as 10 and 7 times; editors' calculation from the raw means 9.5 and 5.4 times); homes, airborne nicotine 0.13 vs 0.74 µg/m3 (5.7 times) and salivary cotinine 0.19 vs 0.38 ng/mL; surface nicotine 7.7 vs 1,303 µg/m2 (found in half of 8 vaping homes vs all 6 smoking homes). UK review: 6 biomarker studies, none from the UK; short exposures no detectable change. Dutch measurement and model (Visser et al., 2019): first breath after one puff, nicotine median 108 ng (below the limit to 2,140 ng), propylene glycol seen in 4 of 17, glycerol in none, nitrosamines up to 77 pg (NDMA equivalent); modelled car / office: nicotine 0.16 / 0.036 mg/m3, propylene glycol 9.5 / 2.16 mg/m3; margins 2.1 / 6 (nicotine, heart rate and blood pressure), 17 / 74–81 (propylene glycol, irritation), 521 / 2,297 (nitrosamines, against 10,000).
lines.reasoning: Observational and laboratory exposure evidence starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on health effects, which is what the sources support: the National Academies, the UK review and the Australian review all say that health effects of second-hand vapour have not been measured or cannot be concluded. The National Academies' conclusive rating concerns the rise in airborne particles and nicotine, not harm. Status replicated applies to that exposure finding, shown by independent studies in different settings.

lines.short: Nobody knows yet. None of the studies we read checked the health of people nearby. Vaping does add nicotine and tiny particles to the air, but less than cigarette smoke.
lines.but: The studies were small and short, minutes to hours, mostly from 2014 to 2017. Nobody followed people nearby for weeks or years.
how: In test rooms, homes and a vaping convention, studies found more nicotine and tiny particles in the air when people vaped, a US expert panel says. The more people vaped, the higher the levels. An Australian review found too little proof to say if these levels harm health.

In one home study, 5 people who didn't smoke lived with someone who vaped. Their saliva and urine held more of a nicotine breakdown product than those of people in homes without vaping. A UK review of six studies found no change after short exposures, but rises after long, heavy vaping nearby.

Vaping gave lower levels than smoking in all four studies that compared the two: in one test room, about a tenth of the nicotine and a fifth of the tiny particles. The US panel says nobody knows what that means for health. It adds that children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease may be at special risk.

A Dutch team measured the breath of 17 people after one puff, then worked out worst cases on a computer. Safety margins were small for some chemicals, like nicotine in a car, but the team called the effects fairly mild. Nothing was measured in a real room, car or person nearby.

lines.statement: How much less harmful vaping is than smoking is contested, and no source read measures it: none compares how often disease or death occurs over many years in people who only vape with people who smoke (the one national cohort read, followed for up to about four years, compared people who vape with people who use neither product; see the claim on vaping and disease), so every estimate rests on levels of chemicals in the body, short-term measurements and expert judgement. Lower exposure is not disputed in the sources read: compared with people who smoke, people who vape had lower levels of many smoke-related toxicants in the body (UK review, pooled analyses: breakdown products of tobacco-specific nitrosamines 58% to 94% lower), and in the National Academies' account of 15 human studies, lasting from single sessions to about two years, people who switched completely from smoking showed better short-term respiratory, cardiovascular and oral measures in all but one. What is disputed is what that shows about overall harm. On one side, the UK government-commissioned review judges its own 2015 estimate, that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking (smoking at least 20 times more harmful), still broadly accurate over the short and medium term and prefers to say that vaping carries only a small fraction of the risks of smoking (McNeill et al., 2022); the National Academies rated the evidence of lower exposure to toxicants conclusive and of reduced short-term adverse outcomes in several organ systems substantial (the committee's judgments; National Academies, 2018); and a 2022 commentary on the Australian review (Mendelsohn et al., 2022), which does not mention the figure, argues that the comparison that matters is with continuing to smoke and cites far lower toxicant exposure, short-term improvements in people who switched and a modelled lifetime cancer risk below 0.5% of smoking's (studies not read). On the other, a BMJ analysis published in September 2015, shortly after the report (McKee & Capewell, 2015), and an editorial (Eissenberg et al., 2020) give the same account of where the figure came from, one meeting of 12 people who rated products by putting their opinions into a decision model (in July 2013, per the editorial), and both quote that exercise's authors listing the lack of hard evidence for most harms as a limitation (the 2014 paper reporting it was not read); the 2015 analysis adds that the chief executive of the meeting's sponsor and the chief scientific adviser of a supporting organisation are reported elsewhere to have received tobacco-company funding (the 2014 paper states its sponsor had no role) and that the panel's selection was not explained, argues that where risks are uncertain the burden of proof lies with those who act and that people who do not smoke should also be a comparison, and offers no estimate of its own, and the editorial argues that the figure should not be relied on now that devices and liquids have changed; the Australian government-commissioned review holds that comparisons with smoking cannot establish the direct health effect of vaping, takes people who have never smoked and people who use no nicotine as the main reference, found no evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease or invasive cancer, and rated certainty low or very low for most outcomes (Banks et al., 2023). Each side concedes part of the other's case: the editorial that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco-specific nitrosamines; the Australian review that people who switch completely and promptly may benefit; the UK review that vaping is not risk-free, particularly for people who have never smoked, and that exposure to harmful substances is similar or higher than with using no nicotine product; the 2015 analysis that e-cigarettes lack some of the most harmful substances in cigarettes, such as tar; the 2022 commentary that human evidence on cardiovascular outcomes is limited, that nicotine may carry some risk for people with existing heart disease and that the effects of inhaled flavourings are largely unknown. The longest follow-up the UK review could summarise was 12 months, and many of its pooled biomarker results come from tobacco-industry-funded trials in confinement of up to 7 days; the funders and interests of each source are given in the anchors and the flag note. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
lines.population: Adults who smoke or have smoked and who vape or switch completely to vaping (mostly short studies); people who have never smoked and who vape; as covered by two government-commissioned reviews, a National Academies report, an editorial, a 2015 analysis article and a 2022 commentary
lines.exposure: Vaping nicotine e-cigarettes (alone, or replacing smoking completely)
lines.comparator: Continuing to smoke cigarettes; and, as a second comparison, using no nicotine product
lines.outcome: Overall harm to health, disease and death (not measured in any source read); what was measured instead: levels of chemicals in the body, short-term lung, heart and blood-pressure measures, laboratory emissions, and expert ratings
lines.magnitude: Not estimable from the sources read: none gives the rate of any disease or death in people who only vape, against people who smoke or people who use no nicotine. The figure in dispute: vaping at least 95% less harmful than smoking, that is smoking at least 20 times more harmful, stated in the UK 2015 report and described in 2022 as broadly accurate over the short and medium term (McNeill et al., 2022); described as arising from a July 2013 rating by 12 experts of 12 products on 14 criteria (Eissenberg et al., 2020; the rating itself not read), and as coming from a single meeting of 12 people who built a multicriteria decision analysis model of their opinions (McKee & Capewell, 2015). Estimate cited on the other side: lifetime cancer risk from vaping less than 0.5% of that from smoking, modelled from what aerosol contains (two studies cited by Mendelsohn et al., 2022; not read). Measured, people who vape against people who smoke (UK review, pooled analyses): nitrosamine breakdown products NNAL 58%, NAB 87%, NAT 94%, NNN 90% lower; acrolein metabolite 3-HPMA 71%, acrylonitrile metabolite CNEMA 94%, butadiene metabolite MHBMA 83% lower; blood carboxyhaemoglobin lower; nicotine not different in 5 analyses of people who vaped and smoked at least weekly; formaldehyde and toluene inconclusive; metals mixed. Against people who use no nicotine: nicotine biomarkers higher; volatile organic compounds not significantly different except CNEMA (over 3 times higher in one study); nitrosamine breakdown products higher in 3 cross-sectional analyses (past smoking not separable); metals mostly higher. As described by the National Academies: smoke constituents 9- to 450-fold higher than aerosol (15 puffs assumed equal to one cigarette; Goniewicz et al., 2014); toxicants 82% to more than 99% lower per puff (Margham et al., 2016); about 1,500 times more harmful and potentially harmful constituents in smoke (Tayyarah and Long, 2014); 4 of 11 metals higher in one aerosol than in smoke (Williams et al., 2013); in people who switched, urinary biomarkers 29% to 95% lower after 5 days (105 people), NNAL down 57% after 1 week and 64% after 2 weeks (20 people); all but one of the human studies showed short-term improvement, none showed more harm among people who switched. Follow-up: the UK review could summarise at most 12 months; the Australian review found no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular disease (21 studies) or invasive cancer (1 study).
lines.reasoning: Observational, indirect evidence (exposure biomarkers, short-term measurements and expert judgement) starts low and is downgraded one level for risk of bias and one for indirectness, which reaches the floor of very low. Worded as insufficient evidence on the size of the difference, which is what the sources support, with the direction (lower exposure to smoke toxicants) reported beside it. The National Academies' conclusive and substantial ratings concern exposure and short-term outcomes in people who switched completely, not lifetime harm; the UK review's statement is an expert judgment on a body of evidence that reaches only 12 months, as its authors say, and the Australian review's reading rests on a different set of evidence. Overlapping reports are counted once. The 2015 analysis and the 2022 commentary, read in full (McKee & Capewell, 2015; Mendelsohn et al., 2022), add arguments about where the figure came from and which comparison matters, not measurements, and change no rating.

lines.q: How much less harmful is vaping than smoking?
lines.short: Nobody has measured it yet. People who vape take in much less of many smoke chemicals than people who smoke. But the famous claim that it's 95% less harmful is disputed.
lines.but: No study we read tracked illness or death for years in people who only vape against people who smoke. It all rests on chemical levels, short studies and what experts think.
how: In a UK review, people who vape had much lower levels of many smoke chemicals than people who smoke. Signs of one family of tobacco chemicals were 58% to 94% lower. A US expert panel found that people who fully switched from smoking did better on short-term lung, heart and mouth checks in all but one of 15 studies.

The UK review was done for the government. It says its 2015 figure, that vaping is at least 95% less harmful than smoking, still broadly fits the short and medium term. It now prefers to say vaping carries a small share of smoking's risks, but grants it isn't risk-free, most of all for people who never smoked.

Critics in 2015 and 2020 say the figure came from the views of 12 people at one meeting in 2013, whose own paper admitted a lack of hard evidence. The 2020 critics say vapes have changed too much to rely on it. Still, they grant that people who only vape are unlikely to die of lung cancer caused by tobacco nitrosamines.

An Australian review says comparing with smoking can't show what vaping does by itself. A 2022 critique says that's the comparison that matters. Against using no nicotine at all, the UK review found harmful exposure the same or higher.

lines.statement: In adults who smoke and had not smoked for at least 2 hours, who were not using nicotine replacement or in a stop-smoking programme and were mostly not trying to quit, in 19 randomized trials pooled from their raw data (a systematic review searched to May 2011; 15 trials with 797 observations for strength of desire to smoke and 17 with 837 for desire to smoke; Haasova et al., 2013), a short bout of exercise, mostly moderate walking or cycling, compared with sitting quietly or a similar passive activity is associated with less desire to smoke rated right afterwards: about 2 points less on a 1-to-7 scale (strength of desire −1.91, 95% CI −2.59 to −1.22; desire to smoke −2.03, −2.60 to −1.46). The abstract calls these standardized mean differences, but the methods compute differences in scale points. Every trial pointed the same way, but the size ranged from a fraction of a point to more than 4 points (I² 92% to 94%), and the three trials that included isometric (muscle-tensing) exercise showed among the smallest effects. Craving was rated only once, immediately or 5 minutes after exercising, so how long the reduction lasts, and whether it helps people stop or stay stopped, were not studied. Participants knew whether they had exercised, the review did not assess the trials' risk of bias, and 17 of the 19 trials list at least one of the review's authors. The review was paid for from internal institutional funds, and its authors report no connection with the tobacco or pharmaceutical industries. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Adults who smoke, abstaining for at least 2 hours in laboratory studies, not using nicotine replacement or in a cessation programme, mostly not trying to quit
lines.exposure: A single short bout of physical activity, mostly moderate walking or cycling (study conditions in the study card)
lines.comparator: Sitting quietly or another passive condition (listening, a video, a cognitive task, body scanning)
lines.outcome: Self-rated strength of desire to smoke and desire to smoke (single 7-point items) immediately or 5 minutes after the bout, adjusted for the rating before
lines.magnitude: Two-stage random-effects IPD meta-analysis: strength of desire −1.91 points (95% CI −2.59 to −1.22), 15 trials, 797 observations, I² 94.2%; desire to smoke −2.03 (−2.60 to −1.46), 17 trials, 837 observations, I² 92.0%. One-stage model: −1.89 and −2.03, with 95% of trials' true effects expected between −3.56 and −0.22 and between −3.45 and −0.62. Single trials −0.22 to −4.54.
lines.reasoning: Randomized trials start high. Risk of bias −1 (unblinded self-rated outcome, no appraisal of the trials, trials mostly by the review's authors) and inconsistency −1 (a tenfold range in size) give low. Worded as an association because the size, and how much of it is exercise rather than expectation, are uncertain, although the design is randomized. Status replicated: 19 trials from several research groups point the same way; agreement with an earlier aggregate meta-analysis (Roberts et al., 2012) is not counted as independent because the trials overlap.

lines.q: Does a short burst of exercise help with the urge to smoke?
lines.short: Right afterwards, it seems to. In 19 trials, people rated their urge about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale after a short walk or bike ride than after sitting still.
lines.but: The urge was rated only once, minutes later, and people knew they had exercised. No study here checked whether it helps people quit.
how: A review pooled 19 small trials in adults who smoke. They hadn't smoked for at least 2 hours, weren't using patches, gum or similar, and mostly weren't trying to quit. They did a short bout of exercise, mostly walking or cycling at a moderate pace, or sat quietly instead.

Right afterwards, people rated their urge to smoke about 2 points lower on a 1-to-7 scale. Every trial pointed the same way, but the size ranged from a fraction of a point to more than 4. Tensing muscles while sitting showed among the smallest effects.
The urge was rated only once, right after or 5 minutes later. So these trials can't say how long the drop lasts, or whether it helps people stop or stay stopped.

People knew whether they had exercised, and the review didn't check how well the trials were run. 17 of the 19 trials list at least one of the review's authors. The review used its own institutions' money, and its authors report no tobacco or drug-company ties.

lines.statement: In adults who smoked, mostly moderately to heavily, and stopped (12 placebo-controlled trials published from 1984 to 2000, with 15 to 240 people each; a systematic review without pooling, funded by SmithKline Beecham; West & Shiffman, 2001), using nicotine gum (8 trials), a nicotine inhaler (3) or a sublingual nicotine tablet (1) compared with a placebo product is associated with fewer withdrawal symptoms in the first week after stopping: irritability was lower in all 9 trials that reported it, total withdrawal discomfort in 6 of 7, anxiety in 3 of 4 and low mood in the only trial that reported it, while results were mixed for restlessness (2 of 5), poor concentration (5 of 9), sleep disturbance (1 of 2) and hunger (2 of 5). Craving was lower in 7 of 11 trials: in all 4 trials of the inhaler or tablet but in only 3 of the 7 gum trials. The review counted significant results and gives no sizes; where a trial did not report a symptom the table is blank, so non-significant results may be missing. Five trials kept people who had smoked again in their analyses, more people dropped out of the placebo groups in three, and one trial used low-nicotine gum as its comparator. No trial of the lozenge was found, nothing is known beyond the first week, and patches and nasal spray were not included. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
lines.population: Adults who smoked (mostly moderate to heavy smoking), without psychiatric or acute physical illness, who stopped in placebo-controlled trials published 1984 to 2000
lines.exposure: Oral nicotine products: nicotine gum, inhaler or sublingual tablet (study conditions in the study card)
lines.comparator: A placebo product of the same kind (low-nicotine gum in one trial)
lines.outcome: Withdrawal symptoms and craving in the first week of abstinence, counted as significant or not in each trial
lines.magnitude: No effect sizes. Fractions of trials with a significant reduction: irritability 9/9, depression 1/1, anxiety 3/4, total withdrawal 6/7, craving 7/11 (gum 3/7; inhaler 3/3; tablet 1/1), poor concentration 5/9, restlessness 2/5, hunger 2/5, sleep disturbance 1/2.
lines.reasoning: Randomized placebo-controlled trials start high. Risk of bias −1 and publication or reporting bias −1 give low. The claim gives directions only; the size of any reduction is unknown. Status replicated: all nine trials that reported irritability, from several groups, agree, as do six of seven for total withdrawal; craving with gum is not replicated (3 of 7).

lines.q: Does nicotine gum or an inhaler ease the first week of quitting?
lines.short: For some symptoms, it seems so. In 12 older trials, people on nicotine gum, an inhaler or a tablet were less grumpy in the first week than on a dummy.
lines.but: The review only counted which trials found a difference, not how big it was. And a drug company paid for it.
how: A 2001 review gathered 12 trials from 1984 to 2000, with 15 to 240 people each. Most had smoked a fair amount or a lot. After stopping, they got nicotine gum (8 trials), an inhaler (3) or a tablet under the tongue (1), or a dummy version (in one trial, low-nicotine gum).

People on nicotine felt less grumpy than on a dummy in all 9 trials that measured it. Overall discomfort was lower in 6 of 7, anxiety in 3 of 4, and low mood in the one trial that checked it. Results were mixed for restlessness, poor focus, sleep problems and hunger.
Cravings were lower in 7 of 11 trials: all 4 trials of the inhaler or tablet, but only 3 of the 7 gum trials.

Trials that didn't report a symptom left blanks, which may hide results that found no difference. Nothing is known past the first week, no lozenge trial was found, and patches and nasal sprays weren't included.
